name: Standard Route (Southeast Slopes)
approach: Primary approach: drive the narrow, one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road (Olympic NP's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft; usually open only early/mid-July through mid-October) 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass, then continue on the Cameron Pass Trail about 3.5 more miles, climbing to Cameron Pass (~6,450-6,500 ft) and the camp sites in the basin below it (roughly 9-10 miles one-way to a base camp, off-trail beyond that to the summit ridge). Alternative southern approach: from Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles since 2002 at a washout about a mile past the road-end parking, some 8.5 miles from US-101, forcing a long walk/bike up the old roadbed before even reaching the Dosewallips River Trail proper and then the multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin — this route adds many extra miles and is rarely used as the primary option today. From Cameron Pass it is about 1.5 miles east along the ridge, with the scrambling mostly in the last half mile (mid July).
descent: Reverse the ascent line back down to the Cameron Basin/Cameron Pass camp, then retrace the Cameron Pass Trail and Grand Pass Trail back to the Obstruction Point trailhead (or continue the much longer exit down the Dosewallips if that was the approach used). No rope work or rappels are typical on the standard scramble; the main descent hazards are loose scree/talus on the upper slopes and, early in the season, glissading or downclimbing residual snowfields on north-facing terrain. Dropping straight off the ridge toward Lost Peak in September ran into cliff bands and fourth-class ground; go back along the ridge instead.
hazards: very long, multi-day wilderness approach with no short options
route-finding on open, off-trail slopes above Cameron Basin
snow on upper and north-facing slopes lingering into late July/August
loose rock, scree, and talus on the summit slopes and on the ridge connecting the three summits
faint, brushy tread on the Cameron Pass Trail beyond Cameron Basin (easy to lose the route)
no reliable water source above Cameron Basin
minimal to no cell coverage in Cameron Basin/Pass

waysIn.name: Obstruction Point Road, Grand Pass and the Cameron Pass Trail
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and gated by the road: Obstruction Point Road is usually open only early-to-mid July through mid-October
waysIn.notes: Read the name on this route with care — it says Southeast Slopes, and Cameron Pass lies west of the summit. The climb is a west-ridge walk gained at the pass. A party that reads the title and heads southeast off the pass is walking into the Dosewallips headwaters. Drive the narrow one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road — Olympic National Park's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft — 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass at about 6,450 ft; the drop off the far side toward Cameron is steep and slick in wet weather or lingering snow. The trail then crosses several unbridged branches of Cameron Creek in a wet meadow — reliable water, and tread that is easy to lose in fog or high brush — to the Cameron Basin camps at about 6,000 ft near 8.3 miles, and on up to Cameron Pass at roughly 6,450-6,500 ft near 9.3 miles. Bear canister required in the basin; there are no trees to hang food. Steep snow can persist on the pass into late July or August and the climbers' path is frequently buried there.
hazards: Route-finding on open off-trail slopes above Cameron Basin and faint brushy tread on the Cameron Pass Trail
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August over a buried climbers' path
Steep, slick descent off Grand Pass in wet weather or lingering snow
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and the ridge connecting the three summits
Obstruction Point Road is narrow, one-lane gravel and closes for most of the year
No reliable water above Cameron Basin and minimal to no cell coverage
Exposed ridge and lightning exposure

waysIn.name: Deer Park and the Cameron Creek Trail
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and it opens earlier than Obstruction Point in some years because Deer Park Road is a different road on a different aspect
waysIn.notes:
The other trail-based way into Cameron Basin, and the one worth knowing when Obstruction Point Road is still closed. From Deer Park, the Grand Ridge and Cameron Creek trail system leads into the Cameron Creek drainage and up to Cameron Basin and Cameron Pass from the northeast.

It is longer than the Obstruction Point line and much of the Cameron Creek tread receives little to no maintenance — parties describe bushwhacking through dense growth, chest-high berry bushes, and log crossings barricaded by jams. Long sleeves and trousers are universally recommended.

Once at Cameron Pass the climb is identical to the Obstruction Point variant.
hazards: Long stretches of unmaintained, brushy tread with chest-high berry bushes and log jams at creek crossings
Route-finding in wet meadow where the tread disappears, with several unbridged creek branches
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and the three-summit ridge
No reliable water above the basin and minimal to no cell coverage
Exposed ridge and lightning exposure
waysIn.whyThisWay: When Obstruction Point Road is still closed; longer, with little-maintained tread and heavy brush, but it joins the same route at Cameron Pass.

waysIn.name: Dosewallips road walk and the long push up-valley into Cameron Basin
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: Recorded because it is a real historical approach — but it is rarely chosen today and is not the recommended way in. From Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles since 2002 at a washout about a mile past the road-end parking. That forces a long walk or bike up the old roadbed before you even reach the Dosewallips River Trail, and then a multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin. It adds many miles over either northern approach. If you take it, the climb from Cameron Pass is unchanged.
hazards: Closed Dosewallips road adds a long walk or bike ride up the washed-out roadbed, many extra miles
Multi-day valley approach with fords and blowdown
The southeast face of Cameron is not a route and the approach passes beneath it
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and the three-summit ridge
Minimal to no cell coverage; long distance from help
waysIn.whyThisWay: Rarely used now; mostly for parties already on a Dosewallips valley trip, since the closed road adds many miles over either northern approach.

name: Southwest Ridge via High Divide and the Catwalk
approach: There is no established route to Mount Carrie from Hurricane Ridge; that area is separated from the Bailey Range by miles of trailless, glaciated terrain and functions only as a viewpoint. The actual approach used by essentially all climbers starts at the Sol Duc River Road trailhead (~2,000 ft) on US-101 near Lake Crescent: Sol Duc Falls → Deer Lake Trail junction (+1 mi) → Heart Lake (+7 mi, 4,800 ft) → High Divide crest (+0.5 mi, 5,100 ft) → east on the Cat Basin trail toward Cat Basin → an unmaintained path over Cat Peak's exposed south side and across the airy "Catwalk" ridge (Class 3) to Boston Charlie's Camp. From camp, the final push follows Carrie's southwest ridge (Class 1 grass/rock) and contours a broad, steep, loose south-facing scree basin around 6,500 ft before a scree-and-snow finish (ice axe advisable) to the summit (Class 2). One-way distance from the trailhead to the summit is roughly 13 miles. Just before the Catwalk the path turns steeply uphill for about 100 ft; it is easy to miss that turn and follow a track that ends in cliffs (early July).
descent: Reverse the ascent line. From the summit, descend the southwest ridge and the south-facing scree basin below it to Boston Charlie's Camp, keeping the helmet on - the rock here is loose and rockfall is the reason the helmet is mandatory on this route - and carrying the axe for any steep snow still lying in the basin early in the season. From Boston Charlie's, re-cross the Catwalk to Cat Peak. This is the crux of the day in descent exactly as it is in ascent: a narrow rock and heather ridge with substantial exposure where a fall could be fatal, and descending a scramble is generally the more hazardous direction, so cross it in daylight and with full attention rather than hurrying it at the end of a long day. From Cat Peak follow the High Divide back to Heart Lake, then take the Sol Duc River Trail out to the trailhead. There is no rappelling anywhere on the standard line. With lingering snow in mid-July you can scree-ski a gully southeast from about 6,300 ft back to the trail, but a washed-out chute near 5,150 ft needs careful routefinding.
hazards: The Catwalk — an exposed, sharp ridge crest between Cat Peak and Carrie; a fall here could be fatal
Thin, crumbly ledges with major exposure on Cat Peak's south side just before the Catwalk
Steep, loose, unstable scree on Carrie's south-facing summit basin
No water between Heart Lake and the summit
Unmaintained, unsigned route beyond High Divide requiring solid off-trail Olympics route-finding

waysIn.name: Sol Duc road end, High Divide and Cat Basin to the Catwalk
waysIn.season: Late July to September, once the high traverse is clear of snow; an ice axe is still worth carrying for the summit basin.
waysIn.notes: Start at the road-end trailhead on the hot-springs road on the park's north side. Hike past the falls, on past the Deer Lake junction, and up to Heart Lake — the last reliable water. Climb to the High Divide crest and follow the primitive trail east from the junction above the lake toward Cat Basin, then take the unmaintained path over the exposed south side of the peak beyond it and across the catwalk to the first camp on its far side. Do not plan an approach from Hurricane Ridge: it is a viewpoint separated from this range by miles of trailless glaciated terrain and there is no established route to this peak from it.
hazards: The Catwalk — exposed, sharp, and a fall there could be fatal
Thin, crumbly ledges with major exposure on the south side of the peak just before the Catwalk
Steep, loose, unstable scree in the summit basin
Early-season snow in the basin, where an ice axe is advisable
No water between Heart Lake and the summit
Unmaintained and unsigned beyond the divide, requiring solid off-trail route-finding

name: South Slopes Scramble
approach: Two standard approaches leave from the Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) area near Slate Peak (~6,900-7,400 ft, one of the highest drivable roads in Washington): (1) the shortest line drops from Slate Pass/Buckskin Ridge down the Middle Fork Pasayten River to Fred's Lake/Fred's Pass, then crosses upper Eureka Creek toward Shellrock Basin below the Carru-Lago-Osceola cirque — about 15 miles one-way; (2) the Monument Creek Trail, also off Harts Pass Road, is roughly 19 miles one-way with more up-and-down elevation change. Pasayten trails are lightly maintained — expect blowdown on the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail and stretches where the tread is fainter than GPS basemaps suggest, so off-trail navigation skill is required.
descent: Reverse the route. In late June the lower descent toward the river from the col was brushy, worst at the very bottom, and the upper scree allowed quick boot-skiing that avoids the Class 3 bits.
hazards: loose talus and scree on the south-slope ascent/descent
long, remote wilderness approach (15-19 miles one-way) with real routefinding required
blowdown and faint tread on the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail
limited water on the high ridge traverses between Carru, Osceola, and Lago
creek crossings on the West/Middle Fork Pasayten River and Eureka Creek can be difficult during snowmelt (June-early July)
afternoon thunderstorms are common on exposed ridges in July-August
steep north face — not part of the standard route, avoid

waysIn.name: The south gully below the Carru-Lago col
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Carru sits between Osceola and the higher Mount Lago and is almost always climbed as one summit of several on a multi-day trip out of the Harts Pass road end. Two lines reach the country below it: the shorter drops from Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge into the Middle Fork Pasayten, then goes by Fred's Lake and over the ridge crest into upper Eureka Creek and Shellrock Basin; the Monument Creek trail is longer with more up and down. Tread through this wilderness is lightly maintained, with blowdown on the valley trail and stretches where the path is fainter on the ground than it looks on a map. The climb itself is short, well under two hours from the base, and unremarkable, essentially a heap of scree and talus with parallel ribs running up it.
hazards: Avalanche debris choking the lower gully (snapped timber, rubble)
Loose scree and talus on the ascent and worse on the descent
Short rock steps and cliff bands within the gully
Steep cliffed north face immediately off the summit crest; stay on the south side
Difficult creek crossings during snowmelt (June-early July)
Limited water on the high traverses between the peaks
Afternoon thunderstorms common on exposed ridges in July-August

waysIn.name: From Slate Pass down the Middle Fork Pasayten
waysIn.notes: The shorter and more common start. From Slate Pass the trail drops north to the Middle Fork Pasayten; follow it up-valley past the Berk Creek junction, then climb toward Fred's Lake and Shellrock Basin below Carru. Most parties combine Carru with Osceola and Lago over two or three days.
hazards: Blowdown and faint tread on the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail; off-trail navigation required
Difficult crossings of the Middle Fork Pasayten and Eureka Creek during snowmelt
Long remote approach, about 15 miles one-way with no mobile service
Limited water on the high bench and ridge traverses; seasonal tarns and snowmelt only
Snow holds on north sides of passes into late July
Loose scree and talus on the ascent and worse on the descent
Steep cliffed north face off the summit crest; avoid

name: Challenger Glacier
approach: Two approaches are in common use, both starting from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of FS Road 32/Ruth Creek Rd off WA-542). Hannegan Pass Trail #674 climbs a well-graded ~2,000 ft over 4 miles to Hannegan Pass (5,100 ft), the last reliable easy water and the split point for both options. Route A - Whatcom Pass: from the pass, descend a steep, deceptively long ~2,500 ft into the Chilliwack River valley (Boundary Camp), ford the Chilliwack River (log crossings here are unreliable and have caught out parties who lost the crossing and had to bushwhack), then follow the Chilliwack River Trail up through Copper Creek Camp (reliable water, pit toilet, ~7.5 mi from the trailhead) and on to Whatcom Pass backcountry camp (NPS permit required), roughly 6-7 miles beyond the river crossing. From Whatcom Pass you must get around Whatcom Peak (7,574 ft) to reach Perfect Pass: the North Ridge direct is loose, extremely exposed, 'a formidable obstacle' and not recommended for most parties; the standard workaround traverses the Whatcom Glacier on Whatcom Peak's east side, which has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses requiring in-and-out crevasse navigation in low-snow years. Route B - Easy Ridge: from the Chilliwack River Trail below Hannegan Pass, ford the Chilliwack again near Easy Ridge (same log-crossing caveat) and climb steeply onto Easy Ridge (site of an old fire lookout), then follow a faint climbers' path along the ridge crest past tarns and slabby sections (mosquito-heavy in season) over Easy Peak to a notch known as 'the Impasse,' continuing cross-country toward Perfect Pass. Round trip via Easy Ridge alone runs about 26 miles; the full car-to-summit distance by either line is roughly 37 miles (matching this route's recorded ~59.5 km distance), so most parties treat this as a 3-5 day trip with camps at Whatcom Pass and/or Perfect Pass. From Perfect Pass (or the Wiley Lake basin), drop onto the Challenger Glacier at about the 7,000-7,200 ft level - the exact entry point shifts year to year with crevasse conditions - cross a bergschrund, and climb steepening snow (a snow arete in late season) toward the base of the summit rocks. A known late-season hazard just below the summit rocks is a moat that has been reported up to ~5 ft wide and occasionally impassable, forcing a detour to find a snow bridge. From Perfect Pass camp itself, getting down onto the glacier can also involve ~200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing and sometimes a short rappel across a moat, depending on melt-out. The final approach to the true summit is a clean 3rd-class scramble to the base of a short (~50 ft), well-protected 5.5-5.7 rock pitch; many parties fix a handline from the summit rappel anchor down to the top of this scramble to manage the exposure on otherwise solid, unbroken rock.
descent: Reverse the ascent line in essentially all cases - this is not a route with an independent descent gully. From the true summit, downclimb or rappel the short 5.5-5.7 summit pitch: a single rappel off the summit block gets a party back to the top of the 3rd-class scramble. A 30m rope is sufficient for this rappel with a few feet to spare (some parties carry a 40m rope for margin, which is more than enough). The anchor is natural/fixed gear, not bolts: 3-4 old but sound pitons plus a fixed cam or sling, backed up or supplemented as parties see fit; check the tat before committing weight since it is exposed alpine hardware, not a maintained sport anchor. Below the rappel, reverse the scramble and handline section back down to the glacier, watching again for the moat just below the summit rocks that can require hunting for a snow bridge. Continue back down the snow arete and across the Challenger Glacier to Perfect Pass, re-crossing the bergschrund passed on the way up; regaining Perfect Pass itself may retrace the ~200 ft of wet class 4 climbing (and possible short rappel across a moat) noted on the approach. From Perfect Pass, reverse whichever approach line was used to get in - either back over/around Whatcom Peak (Whatcom Glacier traverse, watching for bare-ice sections and open crevasses) to Whatcom Pass and out the Chilliwack River Trail and Hannegan Pass, or back along Easy Ridge and down to the Chilliwack River ford and Hannegan Pass - to the trailhead. Some strong parties instead continue over Eiley-Wiley Ridge toward the Wiley Glacier and Beaver Pass as part of a longer Picket Range traverse exiting at Ross Lake, but that is a variant end, not the standard out-and-back descent for this route.
hazards: crevasse fall on the heavily crevassed lower Challenger Glacier
moat below the summit block — can widen to an awkward ~5 ft gap and become difficult or impassable late in the season
exposed, sometimes loose 5.5-5.7 summit block (an alternate notch line has loose, chossy rock)
extreme remoteness — a multi-day approach with essentially no quick bailout or cell coverage
complex routefinding, especially the Easy Ridge-to-Luna Lake-to-Challenger Ridge connection, where parties have cliffed out
aggressive insects (wasps/yellowjackets) reported in the lower forest approach
rapid, hard-to-predict weather changes typical of the North Cascades crest

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass, Chilliwack River and Whatcom Pass, then around Whatcom Peak to Perfect Pass
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The Whatcom Glacier traverse is the season-limiting piece: in low-snow years it has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses
waysIn.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of FS Road 32 (Ruth Creek Road) off WA-542, Trail #674 climbs a well-graded 2,000 ft over 4 miles to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. That pass is the last easy water and the point where the two approaches to Challenger split.

This one drops the far side, losing roughly 2,500 ft into the Chilliwack River valley at Boundary Camp, crosses the Chilliwack, and follows the Chilliwack River Trail past Copper Creek Camp to the Whatcom Pass backcountry camp. Log crossings of the Chilliwack are unreliable and have caught out parties who lost the crossing and had to bushwhack.

From Whatcom Pass you still have to get round Whatcom Peak. The direct North Ridge is loose, extremely exposed and not recommended for most parties; the standard workaround traverses the Whatcom Glacier on Whatcom Peak's east side. Treat that as glacier travel.
hazards: Unreliable log crossings of the Chilliwack River; parties have lost the crossing and been forced to bushwhack
The Whatcom Glacier traverse has been found down to bare ice with open crevasses in low-snow years
About 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing, sometimes with a short rappel across a moat, just to get off Perfect Pass onto the glacier
A bergschrund on the Challenger Glacier and a moat below the summit rocks that can be impassable late season
No bailout worth the name once you are past Whatcom Pass
waysIn.whyThisWay: When snow makes the Impasse on Easy Ridge impassable or wet; it trades that for a glacier traverse around Whatcom Peak, a late-season problem in low-snow years.

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass, then Easy Ridge and the Impasse to Perfect Pass
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the Impasse notch can make the direct crossing either easier or impossible depending on the year
waysIn.notes:
The alternative from the same trailhead. From the Chilliwack River Trail below Hannegan Pass, ford the Chilliwack again near Easy Ridge and climb steeply onto the ridge, site of an old fire lookout. A faint climbers' path follows the crest past tarns and slabby sections, over Easy Peak, to a notch known as the Impasse, then continues cross-country toward Perfect Pass.

Round trip via Easy Ridge alone runs about 26 miles; the full car-to-summit distance by either line is roughly 37 miles, so most parties treat this as a 3-5 day trip with camps at Whatcom Pass or Perfect Pass, or both.
hazards: The Impasse: deep snow moats on both sides and wet down-sloping slabs, with an 800 ft drop-and-re-climb workaround on exposed class 4
Fords of the Chilliwack River
Whiteout navigation between the Impasse and Perfect Pass, where parties have mistaken Whatcom Peak's summit wall for the pass
Crevasses on the Challenger Glacier and the moat below the summit rocks

name: West Route
approach: The hike-in starts where FR-16 (Illabot Creek Road) reaches the Arrow Creek switchback (~2,220 ft) — this is the trailhead, not a formal one. A boot/fisherman's path leaves the road roughly 20 yards west of the Arrow Creek crossing and follows the south (right) bank of Illabot Creek upstream through old growth; it's reasonably distinct and has occasional flagging at the ambiguous spots, but it is unmaintained and unsigned, so expect some searching. Follow it about a mile, then turn right, uphill, at the first significant side creek. The crossing near the confluence can be an easy boulder-hop by late summer or a genuine wet ford in early season, so check flow before committing (it's the approach's main creek-ford hazard). Once across, angle east and uphill through a belt of slide alder and brush (the worst brush of the day) trending southeast, then climb through a band of cliffs and gullies around 4,000–4,300 ft — this is the route-finding crux of the approach: intermittent cairns/flagging at best, and it's easy to end up in the wrong gully. A GPS track of a prior ascent (or careful use of a described waypoint like Point 4593') is genuinely useful here. The last dependable water is around 4,000 ft, right before the terrain opens up; above that, water is snow-patch dependent into midsummer. From there the route breaks out onto open west-facing slopes below/west of Pt. 4593', and you traverse and climb east to reach the base of Chaval's broad west face, where the ascent line's obvious left-to-right diagonal ramp begins. Figure roughly 2,000–2,500 ft of gain and 2-3 miles from the Arrow Creek trailhead to the base of the ramp, with parties reporting 4-5 hours car-to-ramp; the gullies just below the west face are avalanche terrain and should not be crossed in unstable early-season snow, and steep sidehilling with real exposure starts once you're above treeline.
descent: Descent is a reversal of the ascent line, not a walk-off in a different direction: downclimb the same diagonal west-face ramp back down to roughly 4,000-4,300 ft, re-enter the gully/cliff-band system, and pick back down through the brush and slide-alder benches to regain Illabot Creek, re-crossing the side creek near the same spot used on the way up before following the fisherman's path back to the Arrow Creek trailhead. There is no cairned or maintained route for most of this, so route-finding is the primary descent hazard — it's easy to drop into the wrong gully in the cliff band, and carrying a GPS breadcrumb of your ascent (or flagging key turns) is standard practice. The heather- and moss-covered rock on the ramp is more hazardous descending than climbing since holds face the wrong way and the exposure reads more obviously on the way down; a short, steep, exposed Class 3 section near the top of the ramp is where a party might reasonably choose to place a hand line, though this is discretionary, not standard practice. This is a Class 2-3 scramble with no fixed anchors, no bolted rappel stations, and no established rappels — crampons are occasionally useful on lingering snow patches, but a rope is not standard.
hazards: remote, committing, pathless approach via Illabot Creek Road into the Glacier Peak Wilderness (Suiattle/Illabot drainage) — not the Cascade River corridor
steep, brushy, unmaintained old-growth terrain with stream crossings and sidehilling
snow-filled entrance gullies below the west face that can sluff or slide in warm/unstable conditions
exposed, moss- and heather-covered Class 2-3 steps on the summit block's west-face ramp
frequent afternoon thunderstorms in the approach basins
weak/limited water sources on the upper approach

waysIn.name: Illabot Creek Road, Arrow Creek switchback and the west slopes
waysIn.season: Late July through September. The road and the approach gullies typically do not clear of snow until July, and the peak sees almost no traffic outside that narrow window.
waysIn.notes: The trailhead is not a formal one — it is the point where the Illabot Creek Road reaches the Arrow Creek switchback, and you park on the road. A boot and fisherman's path leaves the road about twenty yards west of the Arrow Creek crossing and follows the south bank of Illabot Creek upstream through old growth; it is reasonably distinct with occasional flagging at the ambiguous spots, but it is unmaintained and unsigned. Follow it about a mile, then turn right, uphill, at the first significant side creek. The crossing near the confluence is an easy boulder hop by late summer, a genuine wet ford in early season, so check the flow before committing. Once across, angle east and uphill through a belt of slide alder, which is the worst brush of the day, then climb through a band of cliffs and gullies around 4,000 to 4,300 ft. That band is the route-finding crux of the walk-in: intermittent cairns and flagging at best, and it is easy to end up in the wrong gully. Last dependable water is around 4,000 ft. Above, the route breaks out onto open west-facing slopes and traverses and climbs east toward the summit block.
hazards: a pathless, committing approach through steep brushy old growth with stream crossings and sustained sidehilling
the cliff-and-gully band at 4,000 to 4,300 ft, where it is easy to commit to the wrong gully in either direction
snow-filled entrance gullies below the west face that can sluff or slide in warm or unstable conditions
exposed, moss- and heather-covered steps on the summit block ramp, worse descending than ascending
weak and unreliable water above 4,000 ft
frequent afternoon thunderstorms in the approach basins

name: North Couloir / Christie Glacier
approach: From the North Fork Quinault Ranger Station/trailhead (elev. ~500 ft, at the end of North Fork Quinault River Road/North Shore Road, ~17 miles east of US-101 at Lake Quinault), follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream through a series of named camps: Wolf Bar (~2.5 mi), Halfway House Camp (~4.6-5.1 mi, ~1,100 ft), Elip Creek (~6.5 mi), Trapper Shelter (~8.1 mi, day/emergency use only), a ford of the North Fork Quinault at Sixteen Mile Camp (~13.2 mi, can be thigh-deep in high water), and Low Divide/Renegade Camp (~16-16.7 mi), which sits on the actual Quinault-Elwha drainage divide. From Low Divide, head into the Martins Park/Martin Lakes basin (a side trail off the main Skyline Trail) to establish a high camp on Christie's north side; the broad snow-and-rock couloir leading up toward the peak is visible from Lower Martins Park.
descent: From the summit, retrace the southeast ridge scramble and krummholz section back to the high col. The chossy, poorly-protected Class 4 step above the col is typically rappelled (~30-50 ft) off a sling/cordage anchor on rock rather than down-climbed, since holds are loose and rockfall-prone. Re-rope for the return crossing of the Christie Glacier -- conditions and moat width vary by year and by time of day (softening snow bridges by afternoon), so parties often aim to cross earlier in the day if repeating the crossing on descent. From the glacier's edge, regain the ridge saddle and descend the entry couloir; with good snow cover this can be glissaded with an ice axe for self-arrest, otherwise down-climb carefully as the lower couloir converts to loose rock and scree later in the season. Watch for parties or rockfall triggered from above on the step and couloir.
hazards: loose, chossy, poorly-protected Class 4 rock step above the high col
glacier travel on Christie Glacier -- moat and crevasse exposure varies by year, do not assume it is crevasse-free
steep snow in the entry couloir (self-arrest terrain, runout risk)
dense subalpine krummholz bushwhacking above the col
thigh-deep ford of the North Fork Quinault at Sixteen Mile Camp during high water
afternoon thunderstorms and lightning exposure on the open ridge, saddle, and col
routefinding on unmaintained, trail-less terrain above Martins Park
extreme remoteness -- any injury near the summit means a multi-day self-extraction or SAR response

waysIn.name: North Fork Quinault to Low Divide, then Martins Park and the north couloir
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Firm morning snow in the couloir is what makes this line reasonable; late season it thins to loose rock
waysIn.notes: Every published account climbs the north couloir out of Martins Park to a north-ridge saddle, crosses the Christie Glacier to a col east of the summit, and finishes up the southeast ridge. From the North Fork Quinault Ranger Station at roughly 500 ft, at the end of the North Fork Quinault River Road about 17 miles east of US-101 at Lake Quinault, follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream past Wolf Bar at about 2.5 miles, Halfway House Camp near 5 miles, Elip Creek near 6.5 miles, Trapper Shelter near 8.1 miles (day and emergency use only), a ford of the North Fork at Sixteen Mile Camp near 13.2 miles that can run thigh-deep in high water, and Low Divide near 16 miles, which sits on the actual Quinault-Elwha drainage divide. From Low Divide take the rough fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin and camp there.
hazards: Thigh-deep ford of the North Fork Quinault at Sixteen Mile Camp in high water
Loose, chossy, poorly protected Class 4 step above the high col; conditions change between seasons
Glacier travel on the Christie Glacier; moat width varies by year and time of day
Steep snow in the entry couloir with runout risk and refreezing snow on a late return
Dense subalpine krummholz bushwhacking above the col
Afternoon thunderstorms and lightning on the open ridge, saddle and col
Extreme remoteness: an injury near the summit means a multi-day self-extraction or helicopter

waysIn.name: Elwha side to Low Divide, from Whiskey Bend
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, on the same window as the Quinault side
waysIn.notes:
Low Divide is a divide, and the Elwha reaches it from the north just as the Quinault does from the south. Historically this meant the Elwha River Trail from the Whiskey Bend Trailhead. Since the November 2017 Olympic Hot Springs Road washout, Whiskey Bend has been closed to vehicles, which adds an extra 6.2 miles each way on foot or by bike from the Madison Falls parking area simply to reach the trailhead — check current road status before choosing this side, because that closure is what decides whether it is competitive with the Quinault.

From Low Divide the route is identical to the Quinault variant: the fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin, camp, and the north couloir.

No mileage is quoted for this side because published figures assume Whiskey Bend is drivable and most currently are not.
hazards: Closed road adds 6.2 miles each way on foot or by bike to reach Whiskey Bend
Long Elwha valley walk with river crossings
Loose, chossy, poorly protected Class 4 step above the high col
Glacier travel on the Christie Glacier; moat width varies by year and time of day
Steep snow in the entry couloir with runout risk
Dense subalpine krummholz above the col
No cell coverage and multi-day self-rescue exposure
waysIn.whyThisWay: When approaching from the Elwha or linking a longer trip across Low Divide; the Whiskey Bend closure adds a long road walk each way, which keeps it uncommon.

name: Standard Route
approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (2,500 ft, Olympic National Forest, Hood Canal Ranger District), follow the Royal Basin Trail south along the Dungeness River; at about 1 mile the Royal Basin fork splits off (bear right; do not cross the bridge) from the Dungeness River/Constance Pass Trail. Continue past the Royal Creek and Lower Royal Meadow camp areas to Royal Lake at 7.2 mi / 5,100 ft (roughly 2,600 ft of gain), then about 1 more mile and 500 ft into Upper Royal Basin (~5,600 ft), the standard base camp among the meadows and tarns. From camp, leave the trail and climb talus, boulders, and (early season) snow west-northwest over the moraine rim and across the Surprise Basin snowfields to Surprise Col (~6,920 ft), the Clark-Johnson col, to start the corkscrew route. Alternate approach: via the Dungeness River Trail and Constance Pass Trail to Home Lake, then off-trail through Deception Basin and over Royal Pass into upper Royal Basin -- longer, but useful for a loop trip.
descent: Reverse the corkscrew: downclimb the Class 3-4 slot/dihedral on the north face back to the shallow gully, then descend the loose Class 3 gully to the east ledge (a Class 3 alternative on broken rock just climber's-left of the gully avoids some of the worst choss). Regain the east ledge and climb back up through the diagonal crack -- look for the cairn marking its top, since it's easy to walk past where the ledge appears to cliff out. Cross back over the Y-gully notch on the SE ridge and reverse the Class 2 ledge beneath the cliffs to the Clark-Johnson col / Surprise Col. Many parties instead rig a roughly 60-ft rappel off a natural anchor on the summit block to skip the exposed downclimb. From the col, descend talus and scree back into Surprise Basin and down to Upper Royal Basin camp.
hazards: long, complex approach (roughly 14-16 mi round trip to Upper Royal Basin plus off-trail talus/scree to Surprise Col)
sustained loose rock ('choss') in the corkscrew route's gullies
exposed Class 3 downclimb of a diagonal crack that looks like a cliff-out from above -- watch for the cairn marking its top
a roughly 60-ft rappel is often needed off the summit block
lingering snow on the approach and in upper gullies into July
difficult, easy-to-lose route-finding around the summit block
black bear activity in Royal Basin (bear canister required)
no cell service; a rescue would involve a long multi-mile carry-out

waysIn.name: Royal Basin and Surprise Basin to the Clark–Johnson col
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Seven miles or so to Royal Lake, a mile more into Upper Royal Basin for camp, then off-trail over heather and talus to the moraine rim and down onto the Surprise Basin snowfields. Bear canisters are required through the basin and there are no fires. The corkscrew above the col is the standard line and the route-finding on it, not the climbing, is the difficulty.
hazards: Sustained loose rock in the corkscrew's gullies
An exposed Class 3 to 4 crack that reads as a cliff-out from above
Snowfields in Surprise Basin, icy early and slushy by afternoon
Complex route-finding around the summit block that is easy to lose
A long carry-out with no cell service if anything goes wrong

name: Standard Route
approach: From the Obstruction Point Trailhead (6,150 ft), reached by the narrow, unpaved Obstruction Point Road that leaves Hurricane Ridge Road just below Hurricane Ridge, follow the Grand Pass Trail along open Lillian Ridge, then down into Grand Valley past Grand and Moose Lakes and up past Gladys Lake to Grand Pass (6,488 ft) at about 6 miles. Net gain to the pass is only a few hundred feet, but the trail first loses well over 1,000 ft into the valley, so total climbing to the pass is close to 2,000 ft. Beyond Grand Pass the trail drops steeply into Cameron Basin, then climbs steeply to Cameron Pass (6,448 ft), the highest trail-served pass in the park; the last part of that climb is loose and rocky in spots and holds snow into midsummer. From Cameron Pass the primitive trail descends into Lost Basin at the head of the Lost River and continues to Lost Pass (5,570 ft), the low notch between Lost Peak and Claywood. Parties camp in Upper Cameron Basin or in Lost Basin and climb the peak from there. At Lost Pass leave the trail and head west-southwest across open heather benches and talus toward Claywood, the higher, greyer and more broken summit about a mile and a half away. The final several hundred feet are class 2-3 scrambling on broken shale and loose scree, with a short class 3 step on the west side of the summit block. Everything beyond Lost Pass is unmarked and off-trail, so carry a map and GPS and go only in good visibility. Above Lost Pass a workable line climbs steep slopes and light brush to the 6,068 ft bump, then follows a ramp system on the east side of the summit block; it looks too steep from a distance but goes.
descent: This is a walk-off and downclimb; no rappels are needed. Reverse the class 2-3 scramble carefully on the loose shale, then return east-northeast over the talus and heather benches to Lost Pass and back to camp. To exit, climb out of Lost Basin to Cameron Pass, descend steeply into Cameron Basin, climb back over Grand Pass and follow the Grand Pass Trail through Grand Valley and along Lillian Ridge to Obstruction Point. The loose, steep ground on both sides of Cameron Pass is slower than it looks, and snow can linger there early in the season. Watch for afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge on the final miles. This is a multi-day trip built around a basin camp, not a single day.
hazards: long interior approach
route-finding on open slopes
snow early season
loose, chossy rock typical of this interior Olympic massif
brushy bushwhack-style approach trail with creek crossings between Grand Pass and Cameron Basin
sustained off-trail travel and route-finding beyond Lost Pass — no maintained trail to the summit
no cell coverage; multi-day remote commitment

waysIn.name: Dose Meadows and Lost Pass
waysIn.season: Mid-July to mid-September
waysIn.notes: A long valley walk to Dose Meadows, then the unmaintained Lost Pass path — under a mile and over a thousand feet of climbing, steep and rooty the whole way. Grand Pass from the Obstruction Point side reaches the same high country from the north over Lillian Ridge and down loose shale into the upper Cameron drainage. Either way this is normally linked with Lost Peak, Fromme or Sentinel from one camp.
hazards: Loose, chossy shale on the final several hundred feet
Sustained off-trail route-finding with no constructed path
Loose scree and shale on the Grand Pass side, worse when wet
Snow on north-facing ground into late July
Bear canisters required and no cell coverage anywhere on the trip

name: North Chimney (Standard Route)
approach: Park at the Dosewallips Road washout (~600 ft), reached via about 8.5 miles of FR 2610 from US 101 at Brinnon (closed to vehicles since a 2002 washout). From the gate, walk or mountain-bike the old roadbed roughly 5 more miles up the Dosewallips valley to the signed, unmaintained Lake Constance climbers' path (no official Forest Service trail number — this is a boot path, not a maintained trail). The path launches almost immediately into sustained, root-and-log 'veggie belay' climbing through old burn debris for the first ~0.4 mile before old-growth forest closes in. At about 0.8 mile you pass Half Acre Rock, a large monolith with established campsites and a common water/rest stop on Constance Creek, which parallels the lower trail (by late summer the creek and canyon above run dry, so treat this as your last reliable water before the lake). Past 1.1 miles the brush opens onto steep, exposed slopes, and by 1.3 miles the creek is forced through a narrow defile — the path is shoved up and over a series of rock ledges and short cliff bands, using roots and at least one landmark Alaska cedar as a handhold to gain the next ledge; exposure increases with each ledge and a slip here is serious. In total the path gains roughly 3,200-3,400 ft in under 2 miles to Lake Constance (~4,680-4,800 ft), making it one of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics; a wilderness camping permit is required for overnight stays at the lake. From the lake's outlet, work around/across to the north shore and into Avalanche Canyon between Inner Constance and Mount Constance, aiming for a large boulder called 'the Thumb' that marks the canyon's true entrance; stay low and climber's-left in the canyon rather than fighting scree early. Begin angling up the South Chute — a long, narrowing scree gully — as soon as the twin rock towers called the 'Cat Ears' come into view above; entering the chute at this point (rather than lower) gets you onto firmer, less-eroded ground. From the lake, the South Chute line climbs about 1,900 ft of scree (snow-covered and easier in June, bare and miserable by late summer) to a saddle/notch near 6,560-6,600 ft below the Cat Ears. From the saddle, descend a short ~150 ft, then climb a second scree gully to a ridge notch near 7,300 ft, where the route enters the exposed upper 'maze': either the Terrible Traverse (an airy snow-and-rock traverse above a huge cliff at roughly 7,435 ft — a fall here would be fatal, and in early season several snow pickets are advisable for protection) or its alternative, the Finger Traverse (a downsloping, fingers-jammed-in-a-crack ledge above another cliff, marked by old rusty pitons that some parties use as a solo-belay anchor). Both feed into class 3, occasionally class 4, terrain leading to the base of the ~60 ft summit block, where the North Chimney climbs its north side (3rd class, reported by many as feeling like easy 4th class) to the 7,756 ft summit. Approach hazards: loose talus and scree throughout, route-finding through the lower cliff bands, no water beyond the lake in late summer, and fatal-fall exposure on both the Terrible and Finger Traverses.
descent: There is no walk-off — cliffs guard every side of Mount Constance, so essentially all parties reverse the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb the North Chimney back down the north side of the summit block to the notch; most parties downclimb this short (~60-80 ft) 3rd/4th-class chimney free rather than rope up, and many parties describe doing the entire route, up and down, with zero rappels. That said, a rap anchor (a sling/webbing girth-hitched around a rock horn or chockstone — natural, not bolted) is present near the top of the summit block for parties who prefer not to downclimb it; where used, this is a single, short (roughly 20-25m) rappel and any single rope 50m or longer, doubled, is more than sufficient. From the notch, cross back over whichever of the Terrible Traverse or Finger Traverse you didn't use on the way up (or reverse the same one) — neither is rappelled in normal conditions; on the Finger Traverse the old fixed pitons can back up a hip-belay/solo-belay rather than serve as a rap station, and on the Terrible Traverse's snow section, protecting the crossing with pickets (rather than roping down) is the standard early-season practice. Continue down through the ridge notch and scree gully back to the saddle below the Cat Ears, then descend the South Chute — plunge-stepping where snow persists, scree-'skiing' the dirt sections lower down — back into Avalanche Canyon and to Lake Constance, watching for loose rock kicked onto parties below. From the lake, reverse the steep, root-and-ledge climbers' path down to the Dosewallips washout and the long road walk/bike back to the car; the descent trail is notoriously hard on ankles and knees given the grade and looseness, and parties should budget as much time for it as the climb itself. Net rappel count for this route is best described as 0-1: many strong parties do the whole descent as a downclimb, while a single short optional rappel off the summit block (natural anchor, one 50m+ rope) is the common alternative for those who'd rather not downclimb the chimney's exposed moves.
hazards: highly exposed narrow ledge traverse (Terrible Traverse or Finger Traverse)
loose rock
commitment once committed to the traverse
loose/rotten rock throughout the route, worse when wet or after freeze-thaw
steep, unmaintained Lake Constance approach trail requiring hand-over-hand scrambling — dangerous when wet
NPS records document multiple rescues and at least one fatality on this route in recent years, mostly from unroped falls or descent route-finding errors

waysIn.name: Dosewallips roadbed, Lake Constance trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep; June snow makes the South Chute far pleasanter than late-summer scree
waysIn.notes:
Park at the Dosewallips road washout around 600 ft, reached from US 101 at Brinnon on FR 2610. The road has been closed to vehicles since a washout in 2002, so the first 5 miles up the Dosewallips valley are on the old roadbed.

The Lake Constance climbers' path is signed but unmaintained and carries no Forest Service trail number — it is a boot path. It launches straight into root-and-branch pulling through old burn debris for the first 0.4 mile before the old growth closes in. At about 0.8 mile, Half Acre Rock is a large monolith with campsites beside Constance Creek and is the obvious rest and water stop; by late summer the creek and the canyon above it run dry, so treat it as the last reliable water below the lake.

Past 1.1 miles the brush opens onto steep exposed slopes, and by 1.3 miles the creek is forced through a defile and the path is pushed up and over a series of rock ledges and short cliff bands, using roots and a landmark Alaska cedar to gain the next ledge. Exposure increases with each one and a slip is serious.

All told it gains roughly 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles to Lake Constance at 4,680-4,800 ft, one of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics. Lake Constance is a reservable Olympic National Park backcountry site with reservations for the May 15-October 15 summer season; a wilderness permit is required for the overnight, and parties of seven or more must use the designated group sites.
hazards: fatal-fall exposure on both the Terrible and Finger Traverses
steep firm snow on the Terrible Traverse - several pickets advised in early season
exposed rock ledges and short cliff bands on the Lake Constance trail above 1.3 miles
loose talus and scree the length of Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
no water above the lake in late summer, and Constance Creek itself runs dry
waysIn.whyThisWay: For parties without a bike, or who prefer to walk the five miles of closed road; it adds hours to the day at both ends.

waysIn.name: Bike the closed Dosewallips roadbed
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The roughly 5 miles of closed roadbed between the washout and the Lake Constance path is old road surface rather than trail, and mountain-biking it is a common way to cut the walk at both ends of the trip. The bike is left at the signed start of the climbers' path.

Everything above that point is identical to the walk-in variant: the same unmaintained boot path, the same 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles, the same rock ledges and the same lake.

The same permit rules apply — a wilderness permit for the overnight at Lake Constance, reservable for the May 15-October 15 summer season, with group sites required for parties of seven or more.
hazards: old roadbed surface with washouts
everything above the bike drop is unchanged, including the exposed ledges on the Lake Constance path

name: North Chute
approach: Same as the standard route to Lake Constance: bike/hike the washed-out Dosewallips Road (FS 2610), then the steep Lake Constance Trail. From the lake, head north into Avalanche Canyon; where the standard route bears toward the South Chute, the North Chute climbs a parallel couloir further into the canyon.
descent: From the summit, downclimb the North Chimney/summit block, re-cross the Finger Traverse (or take the Terrible Traverse when conditions allow), and descend the North Chute (or the South Chute, if looping) back to Avalanche Canyon and Lake Constance.
hazards: Avalanche hazard in Avalanche Canyon and its chutes is serious in May-June conditions.

waysIn.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, then up Avalanche Canyon past the South Chute
waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow in the chute is an improvement on the scree, but Avalanche Canyon is named for what runs down it in May and June
waysIn.notes:
Bike or walk the closed Dosewallips Road (FS 2610) about 5 miles to the Lake Constance climbers' trail, then the steep, unmaintained trail roughly 3,300 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camp at the north end of the lake.

From the lake, head north into Avalanche Canyon. This route is the parallel couloir further into the canyon: where the standard South Chute line turns east and climbs out early, the North Chute keeps you in the canyon bed longer and climbs from higher up it.

It sees less traffic than the South Chute and is commonly used as one half of a loop — up one, down the other — rather than as a route in its own right. It rejoins the standard line where the South Chute's gully tops out, crosses the Finger Traverse (or the Terrible Traverse when conditions allow), and finishes over the summit block and the North Chimney.
hazards: Avalanche hazard in Avalanche Canyon and its chutes is called out explicitly for May-June conditions
A long, loose gully with rockfall onto anyone below
It leads to the same exposed upper crossings as the standard route: the Finger Traverse ledge, or the Terrible Traverse's steep snow above a cliff
Less traffic means less boot track and fewer people to ask

waysIn.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes: The alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail. Road-walk or bike roughly 6.5 miles from the washout past the Lake Constance turn-off to the road end at the old campground and ranger station, then the Constance Pass Trail south and southwest to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin, and climb to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif. From Crystal Pass drop south into upper Avalanche Canyon. This is the variant that suits this route best of the three Constance routes, because the North Chute is the higher of the two chutes and coming in from Crystal Pass you meet it without walking the whole canyon up from the lake.
hazards: Unmarked cross-country between Constance Pass and Crystal Pass on talus, scree and lingering snow
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Avalanche and rockfall in the canyon and the chute
Commits to the exposed Finger or Terrible Traverse at the end of a long approach day
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
waysIn.whyThisWay: To skip the steep Lake Constance climbers' trail and enter upper Avalanche Canyon from above, at the price of a much longer road walk and cross-country travel over Crystal Pass.

name: West Arête
approach: Same trailhead and grueling approach as the standard route: a road-walk/bike of roughly 5 miles up the closed, washed-out Dosewallips River Road to the Lake Constance climbers' trail (~1,450 ft), then a steep, unmaintained boot path gaining roughly 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles — no switchbacks, hand-over-hand in places — to Lake Constance (4,800 ft); figure 2.5-3.5 hours. Camp at the established sites on the lake's north end. From there, instead of cutting into the South Chute, continue up into Avalanche Canyon past the 'Thumb' rock feature and stay toward the climber's-right side of the canyon passing below the 'Cat Ears' landmark, following a rough path through scree and talus that fades out below the South Chute turnoff. The canyon is roughly 1.5 miles of steady uphill slog to Crystal Pass at its head; this terrain is loose, poorly consolidated talus/scree when snow-free and considerably faster and safer when covered in firm early-season snow (carry an ice axe June into July). The final few hundred feet to Crystal Pass steepen and often hold softening snow by mid-morning, so an early start pays off. Plan roughly 3-4 hours from the lake to the pass.
descent: There is no established rappel line down the West Arête itself, and no party descends the way they came up. From the summit, most climbers descend via the Finger Traverse or, conditions permitting, the Terrible Traverse, both of which drop into the South (or North) Chute scree system rather than back down the arête. Expect exposed class 3 ledges and a short stretch of downward-facing scrambling around a blind corner on the Finger Traverse; parties caught in poor visibility or wet snow have specifically reported bypassing the Terrible Traverse in favor of the Finger Traverse for this reason. Below the traverse, descend the South Chute's scree back into Avalanche Canyon, retrace the canyon to Lake Constance, then descend the steep climbers' trail to the road. As with the other Constance lines, the only rappel most parties encounter is an optional short ~20 ft rap off a fixed sling/anchor on the small class 3-4 summit block — many parties downclimb this instead, so it isn't mandatory. no published account gives roped rappelling on the arête route itself or its connecting descent gullies; a single 30-60m rope is more than sufficient for the optional summit-block rap if used. Given the pillow-basalt rock (loose and often runout), a helmet and careful hand-testing matter more on this descent than rope work.
hazards: loose rock on the arete
exposure
early-season snow on the western approach
wet or snow-covered rock on the crux hand-traverse section
rockfall triggered by parties above or by melting snow on the route

waysIn.name: Lake Constance and Avalanche Canyon to Crystal Pass
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep, once Crystal Pass and the lower arete have shed snow; firm early-season snow in the canyon is faster and safer than bare talus
waysIn.notes:
Same start as the standard route: the closed Dosewallips roadbed for roughly 5 miles, then the Lake Constance climbers' trail, which gains about 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles with no switchbacks and hand-over-hand pulling in places. Figure 2.5-3.5 hours on that section. Camp at the established sites at the north end of the lake; a wilderness permit is required and the site is reservable for the May 15-October 15 summer season.

From the lake, take the boot path around its eastern shore, come out onto a large scree cone, traverse north across the cone and into Avalanche Canyon. Do NOT turn off into the South Chute — that is the standard route. Instead keep going north up the canyon, past the Thumb, roughly 1.5 miles of steady uphill to Crystal Pass at the canyon's head.

The canyon is loose, poorly consolidated talus and scree when snow-free and much faster on firm early-season snow; carry an axe June into July. The final few hundred feet to the pass steepen, there is often a remnant of ice below the scree fan leading up to it, and softening snow by mid-morning is a good argument for an early start.
hazards: loose, poorly consolidated talus and scree the length of Avalanche Canyon when snow-free
steepening snow and an ice remnant below the scree fan at Crystal Pass
softening snow by mid-morning on the final slope to the pass
exposed rock ledges on the Lake Constance approach trail
cold wind at Crystal Pass
long committing approach with no water above the lake late season

name: Southwest Route
approach:
Crowder has no trail and no road anywhere near it, and the way in is from the north, down the west side of the Picket Range. From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead, walk over Hannegan Pass and down to the Chilliwack River, ford it, and climb onto Easy Ridge. Follow the ridge over Easy Peak, get around the Imperfect Impasse gap (in most years by dropping well below it and climbing back up an exposed class 4 step) and carry on to Perfect Pass. From there keep heading south across the western slopes of the range, below Challenger, Crooked Thumb and Ghost Peak, to the west side of Phantom Peak, then continue south to the col between Phantom and Crowder, at a little over 6,000 ft, where the climb starts. Allow at least two days to reach the col.

The other way in comes from the west and is seldom used: the Baker River Trail, then the high route along Pioneer Ridge, whose southeast end sits at the bottom of Crowder's easy southwest slopes.
descent: Descend by reversing the SW Flank exactly as climbed: down the easy 2nd/3rd-class scree and heather ramps to the Phantom–Crowder col, then back north along the west side of the range the way you came. This is a walk-off/downclimb on the standard route — no rappels are required. Do not be tempted to shortcut east off the NE Ridge toward Pickell Pass: a first-hand account found this alternative deceptively difficult — in practice descending it means weaving a convoluted line of grassy 3rd-class ledges broken by short, exposed 4th-class and even a couple of 5th-class downclimbing moves, past a major chasm/fault splitting the lower ridge, with an unprotectable vertical drop near the base that forced one climber in that party to rig an improvised rappel off natural gear (there is no fixed hardware anywhere on this peak) rather than downclimb it. On the standard SW Flank descent, plan on 0 rappels; a rope is not needed for the reversal, just careful 3rd-class scrambling technique and, ideally, a GPS track of your ascent line given the routefinding-heavy terrain.
hazards: loose rock
brushy approach
remoteness
deep chasm and cliff bands on the NE Ridge — do not use as a descent shortcut
no cell coverage — multi-day self-rescue distance

waysIn.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge and Perfect Pass, then south along the west side of the range to the Phantom-Crowder col
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead the trail climbs about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass, then drops the far side to the Chilliwack River. Ford the river near Easy Creek and climb steeply onto Easy Ridge, then follow its crest over Easy Peak. The Imperfect Impasse, a notch guarded by snow moats and wet, down-sloping slabs, usually has to be passed by dropping several hundred feet and climbing back up exposed class 4 ground. Beyond it, carry on to Perfect Pass.

From Perfect Pass the line stays on the west side of the range and heads south: across the edge of the Challenger Glacier, below Crooked Thumb and Ghost Peak, and along under the west side of Phantom Peak. Keep going south to the col between Phantom and Crowder. It is several days of travel each way, with no shortcut and no easy way out once you are past Easy Ridge.
hazards: Fording the Chilliwack River
The Imperfect Impasse: snow moats, wet down-sloping slabs and an exposed class 4 climb back up
Crevasses wherever the line crosses glacier below Challenger and Crooked Thumb
Whiteout navigation on open snowfields between the Impasse and Perfect Pass
No reasonable retreat once past Easy Ridge; multi-day self-rescue distance
Loose gneiss rock and steep heather, dangerous when wet
No cell coverage

waysIn.name: Baker River Trail and the Pioneer Ridge high route
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The seldom-used way in, from the west. From the Baker River Trailhead at the end of Baker Lake Road, take the Baker River Trail up the valley, then get up onto Pioneer Ridge and follow the high route along it to the southeast. Pioneer Ridge is a long, rough massif, walled by cliffs and slabs above the Baker River and Picket Creek, and its highest point is at the far southeast end, west of Goodell Creek. Crowder's southwest flank runs down at an easy angle to the foot of that ridge, so this line reaches the peak from below on the southwest rather than at the Phantom col.

Nothing about this line is recorded in detail: no mileage, no gain and no camps. Treat it as a serious cross-country route and plan it from the map. Baker Lake Road has been closed to vehicles and walkers from the Shannon Creek Bridge to the trailhead since mid-July 2026 for construction; check before going.
hazards: Long trailless travel on a rough ridge walled by cliff bands and slabs
No recorded water or camps along Pioneer Ridge
Baker Lake Road construction closure from Shannon Creek Bridge to the trailhead since mid-July 2026
Loose gneiss rock and steep heather, dangerous when wet
No cell coverage; multi-day self-rescue distance
waysIn.whyThisWay: For strong cross-country parties who want the southwest flank from the Baker River trailhead instead of the Chilliwack ford; rarely done, so check the Baker Lake road first.

name: South Corner
approach: From the Staircase Ranger Station (~770-850 ft, at the end of Lake Cushman Rd/North Fork Skokomish Rd), the approach starts on the North Fork Skokomish River Trail, a gently graded old decommissioned roadbed that runs up-valley through old-growth forest for about 3.7-3.8 miles to the former road-end/Spike Camp junction with the Flapjack Lakes Trail. Bear onto the Flapjack Lakes Trail, which climbs steadily and then steeply (with one rough slide/washout bypass to pick through) for about 4 more miles, gaining about 2,000 ft, to reach Flapjack Lakes (~3,850 ft, about 7.5-8 miles from the trailhead) - the standard base camp. Flapjack Lakes is a designated, permit-limited backcountry camp, so reserve ahead for summer weekends. Reliable water is available at the lakes and at several creek crossings on the lower trail; treat before drinking. From camp, continue about 1.5 miles on maintained trail up-basin toward Gladys Divide; just before the divide, leave the trail and climb southeast up a steep snow/scree couloir (several hundred feet of gain, often 35-40+ degrees) to Needle Pass. This couloir holds firm, icy snow well into summer, and crampons plus an ice axe are advisable for most of the season - it's the single biggest hazard of the approach, since a slip on hard snow here has real consequences. From Needle Pass, turn left (east) and scramble exposed Class 3 terrain to the summit of Beta Peak, descend through its right-most summit notch (one Class 4 move and a short gully), traverse high toward Cruiser, then drop down a longer connecting gully to reach Cruiser's base, where the roped climbing begins (a Class 4 gully leads to a large chockstone; go left around it and squeeze through a short tunnel to reach the platform below the 5.0 pitch). All told this is roughly 8-9 miles from the trailhead to the base of the technical climbing, crossing Needle Pass at about 5,700 ft on the way, typically 5-7 hours to camp and another push to the base the next day. Fog and low cloud are common on the ridge and ridge-basin route-finding above Flapjack Lakes is easy to lose in flat light, so know the boot-tread line before committing.
descent: Reverse the exposed Class 3 ridge-crest scramble/downclimb back to the top of the technical ground, then begin rappelling. The first rappel drops from a bolted anchor on the ridge crest - parties describe a solid, relatively new 2-bolt station, but also note nearby older rusted 1/4-inch bolts and pitons that should NOT be trusted, so identify the anchor carefully before weighting it - down about 25 meters to a large ledge/platform. From the platform, two more rappels of roughly 30 meters each continue down the Class 4 gully (past the chockstone/tunnel squeeze used on the way up) to reach the base of the route, for three rappels total. A single 60m rope, used doubled, comfortably covers all three rappel distances; a 50m rope has been used but is tight on the longer stretches and some parties add a short bit of roped downclimbing near the top to make it work - bring 60m if you have the choice. From the base of the climb, reverse the connecting gully and the Class 4 step back over Beta Peak's notch to Needle Pass (no further rappelling needed here, just careful downclimbing/scrambling), then downclimb or plunge-step the snow couloir back down to Gladys Divide - soft afternoon snow sometimes allows a short glissade, but the icy, rocky runout makes this a judgment call rather than a given - and walk out via Flapjack Lakes to Staircase.

exposure near the summit

waysIn.name: Flapjack Lakes and the Needle Pass couloir

name: Standard Route / South Side
approach: From the Depot Creek trailhead (reached via the unsigned dirt spur off Chilliwack Lake Road in BC), follow the old Depot Creek logging-road grade south about 3.2 miles (drivable in part, to a washout) to its end, then about 150 yards of trail through old growth to the border obelisk (Monument 65, about 2,750 ft) and trail register, then continue on the fading Depot Creek path up the valley. The first stretch follows an old roadbed for under a mile before it vanishes into forest; for roughly 3 miles the route weaves through timber and brush with no consistent tread. At the valley's headwall (about 3,800 ft at its base to 4,800 ft at its top) the trail parallels a waterfall on Depot Creek — expect a stream crossing at its base, wet slabs, and at least two fixed/dangling handlines on the exposed slab sections beside the falls (a real fall hazard if wet or icy). Above the falls the path becomes fainter through talus and brush in the open basin below Mount Redoubt before reaching Lake Ouzel (5,700 ft, ~8-9 miles and ~3,500 ft gain from the car, 5-6 hours), the standard base camp on flat sandy benches. From camp, scramble up the large broken buttress southwest of the lake (cairned to aid the return); partway up the buttress traverse far climber's-right, then continue up to gain the Redoubt Glacier easily. Cross/skirt the glacier (crevasse hazard, rope up if conditions warrant) to reach the obvious SW basin near 7,700 ft below Custer's summit, then continue to the 8,260-ft notch immediately south of the true summit. A short, vertical, 6-8-ft-wide rock gully (with occasional ice) breaks through here — this is the technical crux of the ascent.
descent: Descend by the same line: the loose South Ridge back down to the 8,260-ft notch, then downclimb the short crux gully (three accounts describe this as a Class 3-4 downclimb; short-rope or a single short rappel off a natural rock/boulder anchor is reasonable if the gully is wet, icy, or a party is uncomfortable downclimbing — trip reports from parties on Custer's south side describe a rap anchor slung around a boulder near a similar snow-gully exit, so treat any rappel here as a natural (sling-around-boulder or horn) anchor, not bolted). Below the notch, retrace the SW basin and Redoubt Glacier crossing, then follow the cairned line down the broken buttress back to Lake Ouzel and camp — cairns were specifically placed to prevent route-finding confusion here, so watch for them, especially in flat light. No fixed/bolted rappel stations exist on this route; treat it as a walk-off/downclimb route with the possibility of one short improvised rappel at the crux gully in bad conditions.
hazards: extremely loose, oxidized volcanic breccia ("choss") throughout — helmet essential, don't trust holds
short Class 4/5 step through a cliff band at ~7,700 ft, with rockfall risk for anyone below
steep, sometimes icy snow in the upper basin and crux gully, especially early season
long, remote approach that starts in Canada, with no cell coverage

waysIn.name: Depot Creek from the Canadian side, Lake Ouzel and the Redoubt Glacier
waysIn.season: Late July through September is most reliable — the crux gully and the upper basin snowfield usually melt out by early August. Earlier trips find firm or icy snow in both and want light crampons and an axe.
waysIn.notes: This one starts north of the border. From Chilliwack Lake Road, park at the large turnout shortly before the steel bridge over Depot Creek, where the unsigned dirt spur leaves; high-clearance vehicles can drive part of it, but it ends at a major washout where foot travel starts on the old logging-road grade. About two hundred yards of trail crosses the international boundary at the obelisk and register, and a wilderness permit is needed beyond it for overnight stays. The old roadbed runs under a mile before vanishing into forest, and for roughly three miles the route weaves through timber and brush with no consistent tread. At the valley headwall the trail parallels the falls on Depot Creek — expect a stream crossing at its base, wet slabs, and at least two fixed handlines on the exposed slab sections beside the water, which are a real fall hazard when wet or icy. Above the falls the path fades through talus and brush in the open basin before reaching Lake Ouzel, the standard base camp on flat sandy benches. From camp, scramble the large broken buttress southwest of the lake, cairned to help the return; partway up, traverse far climber's right, then continue to gain the Redoubt Glacier and cross or skirt it toward the peak.
hazards: exceptionally loose, oxidized volcanic breccia throughout — a helmet is essential and no hold should be trusted
rockfall onto anyone below through the cliff band around 7,700 ft
steep, sometimes icy snow in the upper basin and the crux gully, especially early season
crevasse hazard on the Redoubt Glacier crossing
the fixed handlines beside Depot Creek Falls, which should not be attempted without them when the rock is wet

name: Mount Dana Scramble
approach: Getting to the trailhead is part of the approach: flood damage has closed Olympic Hot Springs Road to vehicles at the Madison Falls parking area, and that closure adds about 6.2 miles each way of road walking or biking just to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road remains open to foot/bike traffic beyond Madison Falls). From Whiskey Bend, the actual hike-in follows the Elwha River Trail, a well-graded historic path along the river's east bank that passes the old Geyser Valley homestead sites (Michael's Cabin, Humes Ranch) in the first mile or two. The trail is mellow by Olympic standards, staying under roughly 2,000 ft of gain through its first 15+ miles, and passes Lillian River junction (~4 mi), Mary's Falls Camp (8.8 mi), Canyon Camp, Elkhorn Guard Station, and Stony Point as it winds upstream through old-growth forest with the Elwha River itself as a constant, reliable water source. Camp Wilder and Hayes River Guard Station mark roughly the trail's halfway point. Continue up the valley to Chicago Camp, roughly 24-26 trail miles from Whiskey Bend, where the Elwha River must be forded; check conditions before you go, since the crossing can be genuinely hazardous in early-season high water or after rain. At Chicago Camp leave the main trail, which turns south for Low Divide, and take the fainter way trail west up the Elwha toward Elwha Basin, past Happy Hollow camp. Beyond Happy Hollow the route leaves all paths: strike north up the valley side, steep and brushy through timber, to the crest of the ridge that joins Mount Barnes and Mount Wilder. There is no path on the ridge either. Stay high and follow the crest east toward Mount Wilder and then northeast to Dana, finishing with a class 2 scramble to the 6,213-ft summit. Water is scarce once you leave the valley floor, so carry enough for a camp on the ridge. This is a trip of several days, and solid off-trail navigation is essential from Chicago Camp on.
descent: This is a walk-off and scramble-down; nothing on Mount Dana or its ridge is rappelled. From the summit, reverse the ascent: back southwest along the crest toward Mount Wilder to the point where you topped out on the Barnes–Wilder ridge, then down the steep, brushy slope to the Elwha Basin way trail near Happy Hollow. The brush and timber below the ridge are where parties lose the line on the way down, so note landmarks where you gained the crest before you leave it. From the way trail, walk back down to Chicago Camp, re-ford the Elwha, and follow the Elwha River Trail out to Whiskey Bend, plus the road walk or ride back to Madison Falls while the Olympic Hot Springs Road washout stands. No anchors, fixed or natural, come into play anywhere on this route.
hazards: deep interior isolation near the Elwha
committing multi-day access with no quick bail-out
a steep, brushy off-trail climb from the Elwha Basin way trail to the Barnes–Wilder ridge, where the line is easy to lose on the way down
unbridged fording of the Elwha River at Chicago Camp
extensive off-trail route-finding through trailless Bailey Range terrain
loose/wet basalt on the final scramble

name: Daniel Glacier / Southeast Slopes
approach: From the Cathedral Rock/Deception Pass trailhead at the end of FR-4330 (elev. ~3400 ft), start on Cathedral Rock Trail #1345 (not the Deception Pass Trail #1376, which leaves the north end of the same lot), which climbs steadily through forest. At about 2 miles, pass the signed junction with Trail Creek Trail #1332 and continue straight; the main trail passes Squaw Lake shortly after. The trail continues climbing for roughly two more miles, breaking out of trees into subalpine meadows and switchbacks, and tops out at Cathedral Pass (~5,600 ft, roughly 4.2-4.5 miles in) at a junction with the Pacific Crest Trail. From the pass, drop briefly toward Deep Lake on the PCT; at a switchback partway down, a use path splits off toward Peggy's Pond, or continue to the signed junction with Peggy's Pond Trail #1375. Either way, the final push to the pond is a rough, primitive 0.5-0.6 mile traverse across narrow ledges with real exposure to steep drop-offs -- go slow here, especially with a pack, and expect it to feel harder than anything on the maintained trail so far. Peggy's Pond (~5,560 ft, about 5-5.5 miles from the trailhead) is the last reliable water and the last established camp; treat water here, since nothing further up is guaranteed. From the pond, braided climbers'/boot paths head northwest and then west across heather benches and talus, gaining roughly 1500 ft over about a mile to reach the broad Southeast Ridge/Slopes of Daniel around 6800-7000 ft. From the ridge crest, the route traverses climbers' trail and open scree below the East Summit (7899 ft) -- faint where it first leaves the ridge, then well-defined -- to a saddle around 7600 ft between the East and Middle Summits. From the saddle, the final few hundred feet to the true (West) summit (7,960 ft) cross a mix of loose talus, lingering snowfields, and the rocky margin of the Daniel Glacier remnant on the mountain's north side. Carry an ice axe and light crampons even in summer -- snow patches here can be firm in the morning and steep enough to want them, and the Daniel/Lynch Glacier ice on the north side opens real crevasses by late summer, so stay on the rock/scree spine rather than wandering onto glacier ice. Hazards worth flagging: the exposed ledge traverse into Peggy's Pond, loose talus and route-finding uncertainty below the East Summit, and possible lingering snow well into July that can require an ice axe on the approach slopes above the pond.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit area, downclimb the loose scree/talus band beside the Daniel Glacier remnant back to the 7600 ft saddle below the East Summit, then retrace the climbers' trail traversing scree beneath the East Summit back onto the crest of the Southeast Ridge. From there, drop the braided boot paths back down through talus and heather to Peggy's Pond -- in early season, lingering snowfields on this slope offer a quick glissade if conditions allow, but check the runout for rocks first. From Peggy's Pond, carefully reverse the exposed half-mile ledge traverse to regain the Peggy's Pond Trail #1375 junction, then follow the maintained Cathedral Rock Trail #1345 back over Cathedral Pass, past Squaw Lake and the Trail Creek Trail junction, and down to the Cathedral Rock/Deception Pass trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling on the standard line -- rope and rack are not part of a normal ascent or descent here; the only technical gear typically needed is ice axe and crampons for the snow/glacier-margin sections near the top. Some parties climb the Southeast Ridge and descend via the Hyas Creek Glacier drainage instead to avoid crevassed ice on the Daniel/Lynch Glacier side, but that is a variation, not the standard descent. Watch for afternoon softening of any remaining snow on the upper slopes (post-holing risk) and for the same ledge-traverse hazard from the approach on the way out.
hazards: Daniel Glacier crevasses widen through the season — by late summer expect a detour roughly two-thirds of the way up the glacier where crevasses can span its full width
Loose, rotten rock on the band between Peggy's Pond camp and the glacier — repeatedly cited by climbers as more hazardous than the glacier itself

Five summits (East Peak, Middle Summit, West Summit, West Pyramid, Northwest Peak) create a real route-finding/identification hazard: topo maps mislabel the "Daniels" benchmark on the East Peak, and the true high point (West Summit) lies past the Middle Summit
Rapid glacier retreat — roughly 700 m of retreat on the northeast-side glacier since 1992 — is exposing more bare ice, moraine, and unstable rock each season

waysIn.name: Cathedral Pass, the ledge traverse to Peggy's Pond, and the Southeast Ridge
waysIn.season: July to September. Snow can linger above the pond well into July and an axe is worth carrying then
waysIn.notes:

The trail climbs another two miles into subalpine meadow and switchbacks to Cathedral Pass at about 5,600 ft and 4.2 to 4.5 miles, at the PCT junction.

Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft, five to five and a half miles in, is the last reliable water and the last established camp.

About 9 km and 2,700 ft.
