name: Lynch Glacier
approach: From the Deception Pass Trailhead, hike to Marmot/Jade Lakes, continue to Dip Top Gap, then traverse west to the shoulder overlooking the Foss River drainage and descend to the outlet of Pea Soup Lake.
hazards: Lynch Glacier is actively retreating and thinning, so route conditions change meaningfully year to year and even season to season.
Standard glacier travel hazards apply: crevasse fall potential and snow-bridge failure.
Rockfall risk on the scrambling bypass used when the moat is open.

waysIn.name: Cathedral Pass and Peggy's Pond, then the east ridge and Lynch draw
waysIn.season: Jun-mid Jul, while Pea Soup Lake is frozen and the moat closed; the lake crossing gets hard once it melts
waysIn.notes:
Hike the Cathedral Rock Trail to Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake) at 2.5 miles, continue to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, then turn left (west) onto the PCT. In less than half a mile turn right (northwest) onto Trail #1375 — do not follow the PCT down toward Deep Lake. Follow #1375 past Cathedral Rock to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft and camp there. This is the shorter approach with the longer summit day, and it avoids the brush of the alternative.

From camp, climb to about 6,300 ft on the east ridge, then traverse below the Daniel Glacier at 6,100 to 6,300 ft toward Lynch draw.

Trailhead to camp is about 2.5 to 4 hours; camp to summit 5 to 7 hours.

From the Deception Pass trailhead, hike to Marmot and Jade Lakes and continue to Dip Top Gap. From the gap, traverse west to the shoulder overlooking the Foss River drainage, then descend to the outlet of Pea Soup Lake.

This is the longer, eastern line into the same basin. It reaches the Lynch Glacier at the same point the Peggy's Pond approach does, and everything about identifying the ice is identical from the lake outlet onward.

A moat at the rock-to-ice transition

name: Standard Scramble (Royal Basin)
approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (2,500 ft, end of FR 2870; USFS day-use fee/permit required), start on the Upper Dungeness Trail (FST 833.2). The trail climbs gently through old-growth forest along the Dungeness River; at about 1 mile it reaches Royal Creek and the junction with the Royal Basin Trail (FST 832) — bear right onto FST 832 and follow Royal Creek upstream. The trail climbs gradually through forest, transitioning to open rocky, brushy terrain above roughly 4,000 ft, then reaches Royal Lake (5,100 ft) at about 6-7 miles from the trailhead (~2,500-2,600 ft gain to this point) — the last reliable, easy water and a common overnight camp for a 2-3 day itinerary. From the lake, circle to its far end and continue past Shelter Rock, a large pillow-lava overhang used as a rough bivy shelter, then through a meadow with a waterfall and along the outlet stream into Upper Royal Basin (~5,600-5,700 ft), roughly 1 more mile and 500 ft of gain — another good camp and water source (snowmelt tarns/stream, treat before drinking). From the upper basin tarn, leave the trail and climb southwest across a glacial moraine (~1 mile) to the base of a large snow (or, late-season, mud/scree) slope on the west edge of Deception's northeast face; this slope leads up toward the Deception-Martin saddle and the remnant Deception Glacier. Route-finding on the moraine and lower slope is straightforward but the rock throughout the upper mountain is loose, rotten pillow lava — helmet mandatory from here up, and watch for rockfall triggered by parties above. Above the saddle, descend/traverse about 100 ft onto the glacier remnant and work westward around Gilhooley Tower and adjoining crags (go around to the west — do not try to climb over) to reach class 2 slopes leading to the summit; the alternate line through Surprise Basin avoids the steepest ground but is long, arduous, and not recommended.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: from the summit, walk the class 2 slopes back around the west side of Gilhooley Tower and the adjoining crags, regain the Deception-Martin saddle area, and descend the same snow/mud/scree slope back onto the upper moraine and into Upper Royal Basin. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble descent with no rappelling required anywhere on the standard route — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rap stations are reported on this line. The steep upper slope is the crux of the descent: several parties describe it as loose rock, hard mud, and rotten scree in late-season/low-snow conditions (not a place to slip — a fall could be hard to arrest given the loose surface), while a lingering snowfield/snow-finger makes for a faster, more secure glissade-and-plunge-step descent earlier in the season. Stay well clear of Gilhooley Tower's east/direct side on the way down, as steep ground there has been the site of serious injuries; the safe line goes around to the west as on the ascent. From Upper Royal Basin, retrace the approach: back down past Shelter Rock to Royal Lake, then out FST 832/FST 833 to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead.

rockfall risk between parties climbing the gullies, especially above Gilhooley Tower
difficult self-arrest on loose rock and rotten snow
exposure on the upper mountain, including a narrow, exposed traverse at the Deception-Martin col described in trip reports as having 'no good place to slip'
complex route-finding, worsened by frequent cloud cover on the summit (the source of the peak's name)
The route climbs a gully on rock that is largely pillow lava -- inherently loose, with rockfall a persistent, structural hazard rather than an occasional one

waysIn.name: Upper Dungeness and Royal Basin to Gilhooley Saddle
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep; before July is preferred while snow still covers the loosest ground
waysIn.notes:
Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,500 ft, at the end of FR 2870; a Forest Service day-use pass is needed at the trailhead. Start on the Upper Dungeness Trail (FST 833.2), which climbs gently through old growth along the river. At around a mile it reaches Royal Creek and the junction with the Royal Basin Trail (FST 832) — bear right onto 832 and follow Royal Creek upstream.

The trail climbs gradually through forest, opens into rocky brushy ground above about 4,000 ft, and reaches Royal Lake at 5,100 ft roughly 6-7 miles in. That is the last easy reliable water and the usual overnight on a two- or three-day trip. Royal Lake runs on an Olympic National Park quota, so an overnight needs a wilderness permit arranged in advance.

From the lake, go around to its far end past Shelter Rock — a large pillow-lava overhang used as a rough bivy shelter — then through a meadow with a waterfall and along the outlet into Upper Royal Basin at 5,600-5,700 ft, about another mile and 500 ft. Good camping and snowmelt water there.

From the upper basin tarn, leave the trail and climb southwest across a glacial moraine, roughly a mile, then up a large snow slope — mud and scree once it melts out — on the west edge of Deception's northeast face, toward the Deception-Martin (Gilhooley) saddle and the remnant Deception Glacier. Helmets from the moraine up: the rock on the whole upper mountain is loose rotten pillow basalt, and parties above you will move it.

rotten pillow basalt throughout the upper mountain, helmets mandatory from the moraine up

rockfall triggered by parties above

name: South Route
approach: Start at the Goodell Creek Trailhead (Goodell Creek Group Camp, ~500-600 ft) off SR-20 just west of Newhalem. The first stretch follows an old logging-road grade/climbers' path along Goodell Creek for a little over a mile before it narrows to a boot-beaten track. Roughly 4 miles in, near Terror Creek, watch for the unmarked junction where the Terror Creek climbers' path splits off — historically flagged only by a rock arrow, a post, and a large cairn, so route-finding here is a genuine crux; the path is well-defined at first but dies out into creek-bottom brush and devils club lower down. Ford/cross Terror Creek at about 2000 ft: the customary crossing is a large log roughly 500 ft upstream of where the path hits the creek, but in high water this log is sometimes submerged and parties have had to scout alternate logs — treat this as a conditions-dependent obstacle, not a given. From the creek, the path grinds directly and relentlessly up the opposing hillside, gaining close to 4000 ft in under two miles through forest, then open heather slopes above treeline — steep and loose in spots. The climbers' path eventually merges into 'Stump Hollow' and follows the narrow crest north to the standard basecamp area near 'Chopping Block Camp' (~6000-6400 ft), the usual base for Southern Pickets objectives. The south ridge starts at the notch at the top of the Barrier — the long rocky rib dividing Terror Basin from Crescent Creek Basin — immediately south of Degenhardt's summit, and it can be reached from either basin. From Terror Basin, climb the Terror Glacier to its upper end (open crevasses can usually be walked around; crampons and an axe are standard here even in summer), then broken rock, heather benches and steep, loose dirt to the notch. From Crescent Creek Basin — reached by traversing Stump Hollow to the roughly 6400 ft saddle near the Chopping Block and descending about 200 ft — a snow ramp rises to the same notch. Parties moving between the two basins cross the Barrier either low, over loose ledges at the base of the Terror Glacier, or high, over moats and steep choss near the top of the glacier just below Degenhardt; both are loose, exposed, and consistently described as 'Pickets Class 3' — sustained, serious, low-fifth-class-feeling terrain despite the modest rating. Total trip is roughly 18.7 miles round-trip with about 600-8100+ ft of elevation range; water is available at Goodell Creek and the Terror Creek crossing, with seasonal snowmelt/tarns higher up that can dry out late season.
descent: Descend the south ridge. Rappel stations are in place where the ridge steepens near the summit, and a single 55 m rope is enough for them; the slings on the stations are old, so inspect them and back up or replace them if you carry spare cord. Because the rock is loose, most parties that roped on the way up keep the rope out for the upper ridge on the way down. Back at the notch at the top of the Barrier, either take the snow ramp down into Crescent Creek Basin, or reverse the loose ground and the Terror Glacier into Terror Basin (crampons still recommended), then return to camp. The Barrier ground is the main hazard on this leg: loose rock and exposed ledges/choss, more dangerous late in the day when fatigued or in poor light. The next day, reverse the full approach — steep descent off the ridge/Stump Hollow crest to the Terror Creek crossing (re-check the log crossing, since water levels and log position can change), then the climbers' path and Goodell Creek Trail back to the trailhead.

waysIn.name: Goodell Creek and the Terror Creek log crossing, Stump Hollow to the Chopping Block camp, then the upper Barrier crossing
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep

Start at the Goodell Creek Trailhead at the Goodell Creek Group Camp, about 500-600 ft, off SR-20 just west of Newhalem. The first stretch follows an old logging-road grade and climbers' path along Goodell Creek for a little over a mile before narrowing to a boot-beaten track.

Roughly 4 miles in, near Terror Creek, watch for the unmarked junction where the Terror Creek climbers' path splits off, historically flagged only by a rock arrow, a post and a large cairn. Route-finding here is a genuine crux; the path is well-defined at first but dies out into creek-bottom brush and devil's club lower down.

Cross Terror Creek at about 2,000 ft. The customary crossing is a large log roughly 500 ft upstream of where the path hits the creek, but in high water that log is sometimes submerged and parties have had to scout alternates. From the creek the path grinds directly up the opposing hillside, gaining close to 4,000 ft in under two miles through forest and then open heather. It eventually merges into Stump Hollow and follows the narrow crest north to the basecamp area near Chopping Block Camp at about 6,000-6,400 ft.
hazards: An unmarked junction at Roost Creek that is a genuine route-finding crux
A Terror Creek log crossing that can be submerged in high water
Close to 4,000 ft of gain in under two miles on steep, loose ground; a torn calf muscle is on record here
The Barrier: loose, exposed, and consistently described as feeling far harder than its class-3 rating
The chossiest rock in the Southern Pickets, with running meltwater over slabby sections as a slip hazard
Old, weathered tat on the one summit-tower rappel anchor

name: East Route / Standard
approach: Start at the Thornton Lakes Trailhead (~2,500 ft), reached via the rough spur road off SR-20 near milepost 117. Follow the Thornton Lakes Trail/old roadbed on a nearly flat first mile to a crossing of Thornton Creek — the last reliable, easy water source before the route goes fully off-trail. From the creek, leave the maintained tread and begin bushwhacking up-slope: expect a series of small cliff bands that force a leftward (northerly) traverse through thickets of slide alder, then a ferny talus slope above a 3,800-ft hanging meadow, followed by a steep, brushy push of about 1,000 ft through cedar limbs and heavy brush to a rocky shoulder at roughly 5,300 ft on Thornton Ridge. Budget most of a day for this stretch alone (parties have taken 7+ hours from trailhead to the shoulder) — it is the crux of the approach in terms of effort and route-finding, not the climbing itself. From the Thornton Ridge shoulder, traverse north over rock and heather, working around minor terrain obstacles, to flat benches near 6,050-ft Thornton Pass — the standard camp for this route (most parties treat this as a 2-3 day trip rather than a car-to-car push). From camp, descend back to about 5,300 ft and cross roughly 1.5 hours of shoulder-high brush to a cascading stream with open bedrock slabs (a second water source); down-climb the slabs about 200 ft, then drop through forest and steep duff for another 500 ft to about 4,600 ft. Traverse into the open basin below Triumph Pass and climb to the 5,500-ft pass. From Triumph Pass, descend a north-facing snowfield to about 4,900 ft, skirt Lake Regret (often partly frozen) on its west-side moraine, then re-climb to roughly 5,300 ft and traverse several miles of heather benches, slabs, and shallow ravines to 5,100-ft Upper Despair Lake. From the lake, climb a heathery ridge to the east, then talus and snow, to reach the cliff band directly below Despair's southeast face/east ridge, where the technical climbing begins. Total approach mileage/gain to this point is substantial — trip reports covering the full round trip (trailhead to summit and back) log roughly 24 miles and 12,000+ ft of cumulative gain and loss, consistent with this route's recorded ~38.6 km distance. Key hazards: creek crossing at Thornton Creek (usually a rock-hop, can be pushier in early season snowmelt); loose, vegetated rock in the cliff bands above Thornton Creek; extended off-trail travel with real route-finding consequences (parties have gotten cliffed out and had to backtrack); and lingering snow patches/steep snow chutes near Despair Lakes into early summer.
descent: The 'standard'/East Route descent reverses the east ridge on which most modern parties actually climb (rather than the steeper southeast-face dihedral line some early parties used). This is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route: parties who instead climbed the SE-face dihedral variant found they had to rappel that single pitch to get back onto the ridge, then realized the East Ridge itself offers an easy, continuous Class 3 downclimb that avoids rope work entirely — this is why it's now treated as the standard descent. From the summit, downclimb the east ridge (Class 3, exposed but not technical) back to the cliff band above Upper Despair Lake; if that band is wet or a party prefers not to downclimb it, a single short rappel (roughly a half rope-length, natural gear/sling anchor off a horn or block — no fixed/bolted anchors are reported on this remote route) is a reasonable fallback, but it is not required under normal dry conditions. From the cliff band, reverse the approach: back down to Upper Despair Lake, across the multi-mile heather/slab/ravine traverse to the Lake Regret moraine, up and over the north-facing snowfield to Triumph Pass, down into the basin, back up the steep duff/slab down-climb section to about 5,300 ft, over Thornton Ridge, and down through the brush and cliff bands to Thornton Creek and the trailhead. Parties doing this in a single push from camp report full days (12+ hours) with the final stretch through talus and brush often finishing in the dark — bring headlamps and expect the descent to take as long as or longer than the ascent given the sustained off-trail terrain. No fixed rappel stations exist on this route; any rope use is opportunistic (natural anchors) rather than an established rappel line.
hazards: exposed Class 4 scrambling with a short low-5th-class (5.0) dihedral near the summit block
loose, moss-covered granite on the southeast face requiring careful hold-testing
dense slide-alder and cedar-limb bushwhacking on the Thornton Creek approach
cliff bands above the Despair Lakes basin that are easy to wander into by mistake, especially at night
lingering steep snow on the SE and south-facing slopes into July
long, committing, largely trail-less approach with real route-finding/navigation hazard in poor weather

waysIn.name: Thornton Lakes, Thornton Pass and Triumph Pass to the Despair Lakes basin
waysIn.season: Mid-summer through early fall, once the snow has consolidated and the brush is passable.
waysIn.notes: A long, mostly off-trail crossing of two passes. From the Thornton Lakes Trailhead the trail runs nearly flat for a mile to a crossing of Thornton Creek, the last easy water before it goes fully cross-country. Leave the tread there and bushwhack upslope: small cliff bands force a leftward, northerly traverse through slide alder, then a ferny talus slope above a hanging meadow, then a steep push of about a thousand feet through cedar limbs and heavy brush to a rocky shoulder around 5,300 ft on Thornton Ridge. Budget most of a day for that stretch alone; it is the crux of the walk-in in effort and route-finding, not the climbing. From the shoulder, traverse north over rock and heather to flat benches near Thornton Pass, the standard camp. From camp, drop back to about 5,300 ft and cross shoulder-high brush to a cascading stream with open bedrock slabs, downclimb the slabs about two hundred feet, then drop through forest and steep duff to about 4,600 ft, traverse into the basin below Triumph Pass and climb to the pass. From there descend a north-facing snowfield, skirt Lake Regret on its west-side moraine, re-climb to about 5,300 ft, and traverse heather benches, slabs and shallow ravines to Upper Despair Lake.
hazards: loose, moss-covered granite on the southeast face requiring careful hold-testing
dense slide alder and cedar-limb bushwhacking on the Thornton Creek approach
cliff bands above the Despair Lakes basin that are easy to wander into, especially at night
lingering steep snow on the southeast and south-facing slopes into July
a long, committing, largely trail-less crossing where poor visibility becomes a real navigation hazard
a full day out from camp, with parties routinely finishing the talus and brush in the dark

name: Standard Scramble (Marmot Lake / O'Neil Pass approach)
approach: From the Duckabush Trailhead (end of Forest Service Road 2510, ~440 ft, reached via US-101 south of Quilcene), follow the Duckabush River Trail #803 upriver. The first ~2.4 miles run at an easy grade along the river through old-growth forest, then the trail climbs steadily and at times steeply (~1,000 ft) to crest Big Hump at about mile 3.9 — the trail's first real obstacle, made looser and more exposed to sun/blowdown by a 2011 human-caused fire that scorched a swath of old growth on the Hump. Past Big Hump the trail drops back toward the river and continues upvalley through Five-Mile and Ten-Mile Camps, with several unbridged side-creek crossings that are normally an easy rock-hop but can be a real ford during spring snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond Upper Duckabush Camp the trail leaves the valley floor and switchbacks up out of the drainage, gaining roughly 2,000 ft over the final ~3 miles through forest to reach Marmot Lake (~4,400 ft), a reliable-water high camp at roughly 19-20 trail miles from the trailhead (the Duckabush/O'Neil Pass corridor runs 16+ miles from the park boundary alone). From Marmot Lake it's a little over a mile more, skirting a ridge with Quinault-valley views, to O'Neil Pass (~4,950 ft). This is a serious multi-day backpack approach with no realistic car-to-summit day-trip option; nearly all parties camp at Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass and climb the peak from there. From at or near O'Neil Pass, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country (no path, talus and heather benches) toward Duckabush's south side to reach either the base of the South Ridge or the south aspect of Middle Peak — both Grade I, Class 4 lines. Snow and small permanent snowfields persist on the mountain's north side well into summer, so the south-side/ridge lines are the standard route; carry an ice axe for lingering snow on the benches and approach slopes in early season (snow commonly lingers on the high trail and upper slopes into July). An alternate approach reaches the same high camp via the Dosewallips River Trail and Anderson Pass area rather than the Duckabush River Trail.
descent: There is no separate descent line — parties down-climb the same Class 3-4 talus and rock terrain (South Ridge or Middle Peak's south side, per whichever line was climbed) back down to the cross-country benches below, then pick up the O'Neil Pass Trail again near the pass and retrace the Duckabush River Trail back over Big Hump to the trailhead. No fixed or bolted rappel anchors are documented anywhere on this peak, and the route is graded Grade I (a route completable, up and down, in a single push from camp), which by Olympic grading convention implies no planned rope work beyond scrambling protection. That said, Class 4 terrain carries real exposure and loose rock, so a competent party should still carry a light rope, a few slings, and some nuts as a contingency to belay or hand-line an exposed step near the summit block, especially if wet rock, verglas, or overhanging north-side snow patches are encountered — but this would be an improvised single-pitch lower, not a planned multi-rappel descent.
hazards: Loose rock and short exposed steps near the multiple summits
Steep snow on the upper slopes into early summer, with possible cornices on north/east-facing sections of the summit ridge in spring conditions
Several closely spaced summits: the main summit (6,254 ft) is the high point, with the slightly lower East Peak (about 6,233 ft) roughly 0.3 mi away, so confirm which top you are on
Very long, remote wilderness approach (20+ trail miles one-way to O'Neil Pass/Marmot Lake, then off-trail) far from help — few logged ascents and no cell coverage
Brush and blowdown on the Duckabush River Trail between 10-Mile Camp and Upper Duckabush Camp can slow travel in less-maintained years

name: Southeast Chute
approach: Two trailheads serve this climb. The Upper Trailhead (about 3,500 ft, at the end of the short spur off Forest Road 2419, pass required) is the usual start from roughly June through October, once the road has melted out. From about December into May the road is commonly blocked by snow at or just past the Lower Trailhead (about 2,600 ft, no pass needed), so winter and spring parties park there and add roughly 1,000 ft of climbing and a few miles to the day; in heavy snow even that lot can be out of reach and a party may have to begin at the Big Creek campground gate. The trail from the lower lot meets the one from the upper lot near 3,900 ft, so everything above is the same. Continue to the signed junction near 4,500 ft where the winter route leaves the summer trail and heads right into the basin below the chute.
descent: Descend the chute you climbed. When the snow is continuous, most parties glissade it with an axe in hand, losing roughly 1,000 ft quickly; only do so in control, because a fall on firm or icy snow, or exposed rocks and ice bulges lower down, can injure. If the snow is hard near the top, face in and use crampons for the first part, and in a thaw the surface turns sloppy and post-holes. At the foot of the chute, rejoin the climbers' path through the basin to the timberline junction and follow Trail 812 down to the Upper Trailhead. Late in the season, when the snow runs out, use the summer trail.

name: Standard Trail (Upper Trailhead, NFR 24)
approach: From the Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24/FS 2419 — the lot has a vault toilet, picnic table, and requires a Northwest Forest Pass), Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is a set of stacked, stairstep switchbacks gaining steadily through forest before the upper-trailhead route merges with the longer lower-trailhead trail (2,600 ft TH, 3.1 mi one-way) at roughly 3,900 ft. From the junction, continue up along the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline (~4,500 ft) around 1 mile in. Here is a well-signed junction where the winter/climbers' route breaks right up the prominent scree-and-snow chute, while the maintained summer trail switchbacks left across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, many switchbacks having stairstep risers that add to the grade. In summer conditions (roughly July–October) the trail is snow-free and well-cut essentially to the top, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes before the final approach to the 5,944 ft summit — total gain from the Upper TH is 2,444 ft over 1.6 mi one-way. There is no reliable water source on the upper route; carry all the water you need. Outside of core summer (roughly November–June), snow typically fills the chute and buries the upper switchbacks, and most parties climb the chute directly instead of the buried summer trail — this demands an ice axe and traction devices (crampons/microspikes), and the terrain is a steep, funnel-shaped slide path with real avalanche potential; check avalanche conditions before heading up, and note that rocks in and bordering the chute are notoriously slick when wet even outside of full winter conditions.
descent: Descend Trail #812 back to the Upper Trailhead — this is a hike/scramble with a walk-down descent and no rappelling on the standard route (0 rappels, no technical anchors involved). When the upper mountain still holds a firm, continuous snowpack in the chute (common well into early summer most years), the popular and much faster descent line leaves the summer switchbacks and drops directly down the chute below the summit saddle: with an ice axe carried in self-arrest position, this is a well-known glissade losing roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes, with glissaders reportedly hitting 10+ mph on good snow. This is genuinely consequential terrain, not a casual slide — an uncontrolled or involuntary glissade, a fall on hard/icy snow without self-arrest skill, or exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute can cause serious injury, so only glissade in full control and bail to the trail if conditions look icy, rocky, or overly fast. Later in the season, as snow in the chute thins and exposes talus and rock, glissading becomes dangerous rather than fun, and the correct call is to stay on the maintained summer switchbacks for the entire descent. Whichever line is taken above timberline, the two rejoin at the signed timberline junction around 4,500 ft. The next junction below that, at roughly 3,900 ft, is a different one and works the other way: it is where the longer lower-trailhead trail splits off, and it is the recorded spot where parties descend to the wrong trailhead, so stay on the upper-trailhead branch there unless you deliberately left a shuttle car at the lower lot. From that merge it is a straightforward 0.3-mile drop down the stacked switchbacks back to the Upper Trailhead parking area.
hazards: Southeast-facing snow chute is an avalanche funnel that becomes sun-soaked and prone to wet slides by early-mid afternoon — start early and check NWAC in spring
Chute-bordering rocks are extremely slick when wet or in fog (official USFS trail warning)
Loss of the trail under snow leads to route-finding onto steeper, looser ground
No water sources on route — carry all you need
Fragile subalpine vegetation on the open upper slopes; stay on the established boot path

waysIn.season: Roughly Jun-Oct, and it is snow-free earlier than the upper road in some years
waysIn.notes:

It climbs steadily through forest and joins the upper-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. Everything above the merge is identical.

waysIn.name: The winter chute, direct from the timberline junction
waysIn.season: Roughly Nov-Jun, while the chute holds a firm continuous snowpack
waysIn.notes:
Not a different trailhead but a genuinely different climb, and it is what most parties are on outside core summer because the summer switchbacks are buried. From either trailhead, follow Trail #812 to the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and take the right-hand branch straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute below the summit saddle.

This demands an ice axe and traction — crampons or microspikes — and it is steep, funnel-shaped slide-path terrain with real avalanche potential. Check avalanche conditions before going up.

It is also the fast descent when conditions allow: with an axe carried in self-arrest position, parties glissade roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes. That is consequential terrain rather than a casual slide.

Wet-slide danger by early-mid afternoon in spring on a sun-soaked southeast aspect
Exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute as snow thins — glissading then becomes dangerous
An uncontrolled glissade or a fall on hard snow without self-arrest skill on genuinely consequential terrain
Slick chute-bordering rocks when wet or in fog
waysIn.whyThisWay: Outside summer, while snow buries the upper switchbacks and the chute holds firm snow; needs an axe and traction and carries real avalanche risk.

name: Standard Route
approach: There is no trail to Mount Fairchild itself, but the standard approach follows a well-defined maintained-trail corridor before turning to off-trail wilderness travel. Start at the Sol Duc River Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Road) on the Sol Duc River Trail. At 0.8 mi pass Sol Duc Falls, and at 0.9 mi reach the Lovers Lane junction; branch left onto the Deer Lake Trail, which climbs steeply and relentlessly through switchbacks to Deer Lake (3.4 mi, ~3,527 ft) — the first reliable water and the last easy camping before things get serious. Beyond Deer Lake the trail continues up through Potholes Meadows (~5 mi) and gains the High Divide ridge crest around 6 mi/4,730 ft, with good views and intermittent tarns/snowmelt for water. At 7.4 mi pass the Seven Lakes Basin junction (4,900 ft) — a good last water/camp option — then continue along High Divide past or near Bogachiel Peak (5,474 ft). At roughly 10.2 mi, leave the maintained trail system at the Cat Basin junction; from here it is off-trail cross-country and boot-path travel only, dropping into Cat Basin below Cat Peak (5,940 ft) and then crossing the Catwalk, the narrow, exposed class 3 ridge linking Cat Peak to Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). Past it, many parties use the exposed, loose-talus sidehill traverse across Carrie's south face; an alternative preferred by some climbers is to stay higher on Carrie's north side, which avoids the worst sidehilling and leads up Carrie's ridge and upper flanks to its summit. The route to Fairchild starts from Mount Carrie's summit: head northeast down the Carrie Glacier (rope up and put on crampons here; ice axe mandatory most of the season), circle around to the north of Fairchild, and climb its Southwest Ridge to the 6,899 ft summit. This final section is only thinly described, so expect to find the line yourself. One-way distance to this point is roughly 12 miles with substantial cumulative gain from repeated up-and-down over Bogachiel Peak, Cat Peak, and the Carrie ridge system, consistent with the ~8,000 ft round-trip gain. Hazards: early-season creek crossings near Sol Duc Falls, steep loose-scree switchbacks on the Deer Lake Trail, serious exposure and loose rock on the Catwalk traverse, crevasses and snow bridges on the Carrie Glacier requiring roped glacier travel (especially early/mid-summer), no reliable water between Cat Basin and the glacier, and heavy route-finding demands in fog/whiteout since the entire Cat Basin-to-summit section is unmarked wilderness travel. In late July the glacier east of Mount Carrie can be skirted along its northwest edge on rock; drop to a tarn near 5,900 ft, hold that height to a gully that rises straight to the ridge, then walk the ridge to the top.
descent: This is a walk-off/glacier-descent route with no rappelling. Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, descend the Southwest Ridge, circle back around the north side of the peak and reclimb the Carrie Glacier roped up with crampons to Mount Carrie's summit, then descend Mount Carrie's north-side ridge. Sidehill back across Carrie's south face (or take the north-side alternative), then recross the Catwalk to Cat Basin, drop to rejoin the maintained High Divide Trail at the Cat Basin junction (~10.2 mi mark), and retrace the trail past the Seven Lakes Basin junction, Bogachiel Peak, Potholes Meadows, Deer Lake, and Lovers Lane back down to Sol Duc Falls and the Sol Duc River Trailhead. Some parties instead continue the descent onward as part of the broader Bailey Range Traverse — dropping south past Ruth Peak toward Stephen Lake/Queets Basin and exiting via the Elwha (Whiskey Bend) or Hoh River trailheads — but that is a different, longer one-way multi-day itinerary rather than the out-and-back standard route matching this route's distance and gain. Descent hazards mirror the approach: crevasse fall potential on the glacier (softening snow in the afternoon raises post-holing/slot risk, so an early turnaround is wise), loose talus on the Carrie sidehill, fatigue-driven route-finding errors in the featureless heather and scree of Cat Basin, and long, tired-legs reversal of the steep Deer Lake Trail switchbacks.

exposed 'Catwalk' ridge traverse with severe drop-offs above loose gullies
steep, loose sidehill sections in the Northern Baileys where a slip could run a long way

name: Southeast Face / Leroy Basin
approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft, at the end of the Phelps Creek spur off Chiwawa River Road/FR-62), follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north up the valley. The tread is in generally good maintained shape, with only occasional overgrown brush in late summer. At about 3.5 miles (roughly 1.5-2 hours in), the trail runs alongside Leroy Creek — a large waterfall visible up-valley from the switchbacks is a good landmark — where an unsigned but well-beaten climbers' path breaks off on the north (true right) side of the creek. This use trail is unmaintained but easy to follow from steady foot traffic; it climbs very steeply, gaining roughly 2,000 ft in about 1.5-1.9 miles while staying above Leroy Creek, which is the last reliable water before the basin. It eases into Leroy Creek Basin (~6,050-6,100 ft, about 5.4 mi and ~2,700 ft gain from the trailhead), a broad heather-and-boulder cirque that is the standard base camp, with good tent sites and running water. From camp most parties continue north/northeast across meadow and rock toward a col (~7,800 ft) on Seven Fingered Jack's south shoulder, roughly another hour. This whole upper section is cross-country with sparse cairns — Fernow itself isn't visible from most of Leroy Basin, and the peak has a well-earned reputation for tricky route-finding, so carry a map/GPS track rather than counting on a visible target. From the col, the route loses about 1,000 ft into the basin below the Gloomy Glacier, crossing beneath a shrinking glacier remnant (open crevasses have been reported here — rope up for the crossing or give it a wide berth), then climbs the broad talus/scree slopes below Fernow's summit, roughly a mile toward the summit block, mostly class 2-3 talus with one notably exposed 'unexpected crux' — a sloped, gravel-covered slab with about a 30 m drop below and a 10 m traverse across it, rated only class 2 but consequential.
descent: Descend the same line used on ascent — Fernow's summit sits atop a maze of loose gullies and there is no reliable shortcut. From the top, downclimb the class 4 (occasionally low 5th, but the harder moves can be sidestepped) summit block; some parties, especially in wet rock or with a less experienced group, sling a horn or block on the north side of the block for a quick single rappel instead of downclimbing the crux moves — there are no fixed or bolted anchors on this route, so bring a couple of slings/rap rings to build a natural anchor, and a 30 m rope is sufficient (it's used to protect just the short crux section, not to reach the ground, so most parties still downclimb the remainder). Below the block, retrace the choss gully to about 8,800 ft, re-cross the exposed sloped-slab traverse with care (more consequential descending than ascending), then continue down the talus/scree valley back toward the glacier remnant, watching again for the crevasse near the plateau. From there you must reclimb roughly 1,000 ft back up to the Seven Fingered Jack col before dropping into Leroy Basin; an alternate some parties use off the col instead drops climber's-right across sandy ledges and down through large boulders directly to the basin, trading the reclimb for its own loose, ankle-twisting terrain. The descent is worse underfoot than the climb up — expect a great deal of loose rock, near-misses, and slips — so wear a helmet the whole way and plan to be off the summit block and crux traverse before dark. From Leroy Basin, reverse the steep climbers' trail back down to Phelps Creek Trail #1511 and out to the trailhead. Because the round trip from Leroy Basin alone can run 10-13+ hours, most parties treat the climb as a 2-3 day trip, camping at Leroy Basin going in and out rather than pushing car-to-car in a day.
hazards: loose scree and talus throughout Leroy Basin, the Seven Fingered Jack ridge, and Fernow itself
rockfall in gullies and benches, worsened by other parties above on this popular multi-peak objective
exposed, unavoidable class 4 (occasionally low 5th class) moves on the final summit block
hidden crevasses/moats under talus and late-season snow near the Gloomy Glacier remnant
long approach with complex cross-country route-finding and significant elevation gain
afternoon thunderstorms common on the open upper ridge in summer

waysIn.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing runs through avalanche terrain earlier than that
waysIn.notes:
Same walk in as for Seven Fingered Jack and Maude: Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft, then the steep unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft.

This is the common approach but not the elegant one. All three ways in converge on the same south-east face finish.

From Leroy Basin, head north-west toward a waterfall and climb its left side to a small notch on the ridge of Seven Fingered Jack. Published descriptions of this saddle vary — one places it just west of an obvious 7,700 ft col with a couple of bivy sites at the low point, another gives it as a notch reached past a second creek crossing — and they may or may not be the same feature, so check it on a map rather than assuming.

From the saddle you must drop about a thousand feet into the moraine at the terminus of the Gloomy Glacier, and every foot of it has to be regained on the way out. Two published ways down: descend to the tarn below and go around a prominent rock formation that guards the basin, or descend to the right across sandy ledges and down large boulders.

Expect roughly nine hours round trip from Leroy Basin, and a very long day car to car — one party left the trailhead at three in the morning and got back at eleven at night.
hazards: Route-finding is the crux: Fernow is not visible from Leroy Basin and cairns are sparse
About a thousand feet of descent from the col into the Gloomy basin that must be regained on the way out
Open crevasses and icy slopes at the Gloomy Glacier remnant; rope up or give it a wide berth
Avalanche terrain on the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing earlier in the season
Roughly two thousand feet of exceptionally loose talus and scree above the basin
Exposed gravel-covered sloped slab traverse (about 30 m drop) and narrow exposed ledges off the col; avoidable
Exposed class 4 (occasionally low 5th) moves on the final summit block
Afternoon thunderstorms on the open upper ridge

waysIn.name: Holden Village and Copper Basin
waysIn.notes: From Holden Village up to the Copper–Entiat divide and the east ridge. The most direct way to the standard east-side line, and climbable in a day from Holden, but it depends on the Lake Chelan boat. The ferry up Lake Chelan to Holden and the Railroad Creek trail into Copper Basin gains the East Ridge — the standard route — much more directly than the Leroy Basin approach.

Boat-dependent access via Lake Chelan to Holden
waysIn.whyThisWay: When you can take the Lake Chelan boat to Holden; it reaches the standard east-side line more directly and can be done in a day from the village.

waysIn.name: Entiat River from Cottonwood
waysIn.notes: Up the Entiat River trail toward the Entiat Glacier and the east ridge. The longest way in, with less gain and little avalanche exposure. It reaches the East Ridge by way of the Entiat Glacier.

Entiat Glacier crossing; crevasses and glacier recession can change conditions (unconfirmed for this variant)

waysIn.whyThisWay: For a long, mostly trail approach with less gain and little avalanche exposure, when the Phelps Creek approach is in avalanche condition or you are making a longer trip.

name: South Slopes (Bailey Range)
approach: There is no dedicated trailhead, road, or maintained path to Mount Ferry — reaching it means committing to 2-3 days of the Bailey Range Traverse, Olympic National Park's classic off-trail high route that links the Sol Duc River trailhead (via Sol Duc Falls Trail #630) in the north with the Elwha River/Whiskey Bend trailhead in the south, or with the North Fork Quinault trailhead via Dodwell-Rixon Pass on the longer loop variant. The most common approach starts at the Sol Duc Trailhead: maintained trail runs about 1 mile to Sol Duc Falls, then climbs steadily past Deer Lake and up the High Divide Trail toward Bogachiel Peak/Heart Lake — roughly 9-11 miles and ~3,300 ft of gain from the car, and the last reliable on-trail water and camp before travel goes off-trail. From High Divide near Cat Basin, the route leaves the maintained trail and follows the Bailey Range crest east: over Cat Peak's exposed 'Catwalk' (an airy class 3 knife-edge ridge, the first of two such sections on the traverse) and Stephen Peak, where steep heather benches with class 3-4 moves lead into a second, brushier catwalk with awkward gully crossings serious enough to warrant a blunt 'don't. Fall.' warning before dropping into Ferry Basin (~5,700 ft), the standard camp beneath Mount Ferry and roughly 2 days / 15-20 miles of travel in. Ferry Basin has dependable water — a small waterfall about 60 ft from the usual camp spot, plus a nearby tarn — and is often considered one of the nicer camps on the traverse. From camp, Ferry's summit is reached via a broad bench and scree/talus slope east of the true summit, loose 'dagger scree' (sharp, shifting shale-like rock) that demands careful footing but involves no technical climbing, just sustained off-trail scrambling. A less-common southern approach comes in via Dodwell-Rixon Pass and Queets Basin, up Ball Bearing Gully to the Scott-Ludden saddle, then along the Ferry-Ludden ridge to that same broad bench east of the summit. Either way, expect no signage, no bridges, unmarked creek fords, lingering snow/ice in gullies and on north-facing slopes even in August (ice axe and often crampons are standard kit), slide alder brush lower on the flanks, and serious route-finding responsibility — this is remote, high alpine terrain well beyond the maintained trail network.
descent: Mount Ferry has no rappels and no technical descent — it is a scramble summit reached and left entirely on foot, so treat rappels as 0. The standard way down reverses the ascent scree/talus slope on the peak's southeast side, which parties describe as distinctly easier than the way up — practically a stroll on milder, more consolidated ground compared to the loose dagger scree above Ferry Basin — dropping back onto the broad bench and rejoining the Bailey Range crest route. From there, parties continuing the traverse typically down-climb roughly 200 ft through a small connecting canyon southwest to the Ferry-Pulitzer saddle to press on toward Mount Pulitzer and eventually Bear Pass, while parties treating Ferry as an out-and-back reverse the route back to Ferry Basin camp and retrace the catwalks over Stephen and Cat Peaks to High Divide and the Sol Duc Trailhead. Parties continuing the full traverse southward instead drop via Dodwell-Rixon Pass into Queets Basin and the Elwha headwaters, eventually exiting via the Elwha Snowfinger — historically a reliable permanent snowfield but now reportedly in shambles, requiring steep, slippery side-hilling on grass and talus above the canyon plus stream crossings rather than a straightforward snow glissade; this exit is consistently rated among the hardest days of the traverse. Whichever way you leave Ferry, expect the same hazards as the approach in reverse: loose scree, exposed class 3-4 moves on the catwalks, lingering snow/ice in shaded gullies, and multi-day off-trail route-finding with no cell coverage until you rejoin High Divide or a trailhead road.

exposure on traverse sections (notably 'The Catwalk,' a 1-2 ft-wide exposed ridge crest between Cat Basin and Mount Carrie)
afternoon weather and thunderstorm buildup
Elwha Snowfinger exit has largely melted out and is no longer reliably passable (2023-2025 reports) -- do not rely on it as a bailout

waysIn.name: Bailey Range crest to Ferry Basin
waysIn.season: Late July to mid-September
waysIn.notes: Days of off-trail travel: Sol Duc and the High Divide to the last dependable water, then the Bailey crest east over Cat Peak's catwalk and Stephen Peak, with steep heather benches and awkward gully crossings before the drop into Ferry Basin. A southern line comes in over Dodwell-Rixon Pass and Queets Basin, up Ball Bearing Gully to the Scott–Ludden saddle and along the Ferry–Ludden ridge.
hazards: Loose plate-like scree on the final slope that shifts underfoot
Exposed Class 3 to 4 moves on the catwalks between Cat, Carrie and Stephen
Snow and ice in shaded gullies and north-facing slopes even in August
A maze of faint elk trails in the basin that read as the route and are not
Multi-day off-trail commitment with no signage, bridges or coverage

name: Standard Scramble (Constance Pass / Home Lake)
approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (~2,880 ft, end of FR 2870), follow the Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 south along the Dungeness River. The first mile is mostly flat; stay left at the Royal Basin Trail junction near 1 mile, and reach Camp Handy (riverside meadow with a cedar shingle shelter, a popular camp) at about 3.4 miles. Just past Camp Handy the trail forks — take the uphill fork and begin a sustained, largely switchback-free climb through forest for about 3 more miles, gaining roughly 1,800 ft, to Boulder Shelter (6.4 mi, ~4,890 ft). The creek at Boulder Shelter is the most reliable water source on the whole approach, so treat it as your last sure fill-up before the high country — there are two more reported water sources between Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter but they can be seasonal. At Boulder Shelter, bear right to join the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail; the Olympic National Park boundary is crossed about 1 mile beyond the shelter. The final ~2.9 miles to Home Lake (5,330 ft, roughly 9.3–9.6 mi from the trailhead) climb another 700–900 ft through subalpine forest into heather meadows, crossing two to three small streams/snowmelt runnels — trip reports flag one waterfall crossing on this stretch as a bit dicey for keeping feet dry, and it can be slick with a full pack in early season. Home Lake, in a basin just below Constance Pass, is the standard base camp for Fricaba, Hal Foss, Mystery, and Deception. From camp, continue on climbers' paths (no maintained tread) up to Constance Pass (~5,750 ft), then traverse/descend west into upper Deception Basin before turning toward the Fricaba–Hal Foss col and ascending loose scree/talus on Fricaba's SW or North ridge (the two most commonly ascended of its five ridges) to the summit. The rock here is extremely shattered, rotten shale typical of this corner of the Olympics — expect two steps up and one slide back, real rockfall/ankle-turn hazard, some Class 2–3 scrambling near the ridge crest, and lingering snow on the Constance Pass–Deception Basin traverse into July that can require an ice axe.
descent: Descend the same way you came up: reverse the scree/talus ridge line down to the Fricaba–Hal Foss col, drop back into Deception Basin, climb back over Constance Pass, and descend to Home Lake (or continue the full ~9.6 miles out to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead if pushing it car-to-car in a day — most parties instead camp at Home Lake or in Deception Basin and hike out the next day). This is a non-technical walk-off/downclimb — Fricaba is consistently described as a fairly easy scramble and a scree walkup on shattered, rotten shale, and no fixed rappel anchors or technical rappel stations are reported on the North or SW ridge lines (unlike neighboring Mount Constance, which has a rap station off its summit). The main descent hazards are loose rock and ankle-turning scree underfoot in the rotten Fricaba rock, brief exposed Class 3 downclimbing moves near the ridge crest/col, and — in early season — glissading or firm snow on the Constance Pass/Deception Basin traverse, where an ice axe is recommended into early summer. Late September: on the way down the summit ridge, stay on the north side; a lower path there skips the towers and is far less exposed.
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes
Lingering steep snow in the approach basins into early summer
Long, committing backcountry approach far from help

waysIn.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake and Constance Pass
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Oct per NPS guidance for the Constance Pass and Home Lake corridor; earlier trips should expect lingering snow
waysIn.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,880 ft at the end of FR 2870, follow Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 south along the Dungeness River. The first mile is mostly flat; stay left at the Royal Basin Trail junction near a mile. Camp Handy — riverside meadow with a cedar shingle shelter — comes at about 3.4 miles.

Just past Camp Handy the trail forks; take the uphill fork and begin a sustained, largely switchback-free climb of about 3 miles and 1,800 ft to Boulder Shelter at 6.4 miles and about 4,890 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the whole approach — treat it as the last sure fill-up. Bear right at the shelter onto the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail. The park boundary is about a mile beyond, after which brush closes in from both sides.

The final 2.9 miles to Home Lake at 5,330 ft, roughly 9.3-9.6 miles from the trailhead, climb another 700-900 ft through subalpine forest into heather meadows, crossing two or three small streams; one waterfall crossing is awkward to keep feet dry and is slick with a full pack early season. Home Lake is the standard basecamp for Fricaba, Hal Foss, Mystery and Deception.

From camp continue on climbers' paths — no maintained tread — up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, then traverse and descend west into upper Deception Basin.
hazards: Extremely shattered rotten shale with real rockfall and ankle-turn hazard the whole way up
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes, with the steepest 500-600 ft immediately off the pass
Lingering steep snow on the Constance Pass to Deception Basin traverse into July, warranting an axe
Brief exposed Class 3 downclimbing near the ridge crest and col on the way out
A long, committing backcountry approach far from help
Boulder Shelter sits at the foot of an avalanche chute with snapped trees in the scar

waysIn.name: Royal Basin and the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The other way into the same basin, and the one that suits a party doing Fricaba alongside Mystery and Deception. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead take Trail #833.2 about a mile and bear right onto the Royal Basin Trail #832 at the fork just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the basecamp; upper Royal Basin camps sit around 5,800-6,200 ft.

From upper Royal Basin climb the moraine and a 35-40 degree snowfield to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend scree to the grass and heather benches above Deception Basin. Fricaba is then across the basin to the east.

One published day-2 description of this side has parties angling up toward the pass going east for Fricaba, then round to the left of some gendarmes and up a steep scree route the account calls self-explanatory.
hazards: A 35-40 degree snowfield below the Royal-Deception notch, wanting an axe outside late season
Shattered shale and scree on Fricaba itself
Gendarmes on the approach ridge that must be skirted rather than climbed
Long approach with the last dependable water at Royal Lake
waysIn.whyThisWay: When combining Fricaba with Mystery, Deception or Hal Foss, camping at Royal Lake and crossing a snowfield to the divide, rather than the longer walk to Home Lake.

name: Southeast Glaciers (Standard)
approach: From the Ross Dam Trailhead at Happy Flats on SR 20 (~milepost 134, 2,150 ft), it's about 1 mile down to the Ross Lake water taxi dock; cross the lake by taxi (or paddle) to Big Beaver Landing. From the landing, follow the Big Beaver Creek Trail 11.5 miles up-valley — a dry, well-maintained, largely flat trail taking roughly 5 hours, passing Luna Camp around the 4.7-hour mark. About 29 minutes beyond Luna Camp, a large (~15-inch-diameter) log crossing of Big Beaver Creek marks the turnoff: leave the trail here and head up the Access Creek drainage. This next mile is a real bushwhack, gaining roughly 1,900 ft (2,400 ft to 4,300 ft): start in valley-bottom devil's club, cross to the creek's north side around 3,800 ft where brush pinches in on both banks, then climb through moderately dense huckleberry brush before the final half-mile of talus into Access Basin — watch for deadfall, thick undercover, and biting insects. From Access Basin, a long, steep, loose scree chute gains ~1,800 ft to 6,100-ft Access Col (2-3 hours; can be brutally hot with no shade in the chute). From the col, traverse notoriously steep heather (an axe is worthwhile for security on the short, steep sections) and talus to Luna Pass, where most parties camp near lingering snow patches for water. From Luna Pass, skirt a rock knob that towers ~100 ft over the pass via a broad ledge on its northwest face to reach the surprisingly gentle Northeast Ridge crest, then follow the ridge's many short ups and downs — including a ~25-ft rock step with a climbable vertical crack (Class 3) — toward Fury. Where the ridge crest drops away, descend a steep, narrow heather chute (~500 ft) into a talus basin around 6,500 ft, then contour southwest across talus, heather, and polished slabs to a rocky rib that blocks easy passage; the lower of two ledge options (exposed scrambling on wet, mossy rock and steep heather) is generally preferred to the looser, more exposed upper ledge.
descent: This is fundamentally a walk-off/downclimb along the ascent line, not a rappel-heavy route, though one short technical step is often rappelled. From the summit, reverse the steep snowfield on a running belay with flukes (take particular care on the upper, firmer section — crampon-balling on wet snow has been reported), then retrace the Southeast Glacier descent, working back around the bergschrund. Regain the Northeast Ridge crest (parties often angle up sooner than the ascent line to save time) and reverse the rocky-rib traverse and heather-chute climb back to the ridge. At the ~25-ft rock step, many parties opt for a short single-pitch rappel rather than downclimbing the crack — a single 30m (or even shorter) rope is plenty, and the anchor is whatever natural gear (cams/nuts/slings on a horn or chockstone) the party builds, as there is no fixed/bolted station reported at this feature. From there, finish the ridge traverse back to Luna Pass. The following day, reverse the full approach: the heather/talus traverse and scree descent back to Access Col, the steep 1,800-ft drop into Access Basin, the Access Creek bushwhack (often taken as a more direct, steeper line straight down the brushy hillside rather than retracing the ascent line) back to the Big Beaver Creek log crossing, then the 11.5-mile Big Beaver Creek Trail out to the water taxi landing and back across Ross Lake to the Ross Dam Trailhead. One party took roughly 6 hours from the summit back to Luna Pass camp, and made the full round trip (camp to camp to trailhead) as a 4-day, ~42-mile, ~13,000 ft trip.

rockfall
navigation in whiteout
extreme isolation
moat/bergschrund crossing at the glacier's rock margin (documented fall/rescue site, June 2025)
dense brush and devil's club on the Access Creek approach
loose Class 4-5 rock bands on the ridge and glacier margins
early-season steep snow (up to ~50°) that can persist into July

waysIn.name: Ross Lake water taxi, Big Beaver Creek Trail, the Access Creek bushwhack, Access Col and Luna Pass
waysIn.season: Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at Happy Flats on SR-20 near milepost 134 at 2,150 ft, walk about a mile down to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock and cross to Big Beaver Landing. From the landing, 11.5 miles of dry, well-maintained, largely flat trail up-valley takes roughly 5 hours, passing Luna Camp at about the 4.7-hour mark.

About 29 minutes beyond Luna Camp a large log crossing of Big Beaver Creek, roughly 15 inches in diameter, marks the turnoff. Leave the trail there and head up Access Creek: a real bushwhack of about a mile gaining 1,900 ft, starting in valley-bottom devil's club, crossing to the creek's north side around 3,800 ft where brush pinches in on both banks, then huckleberry and a final half-mile of talus into Access Basin.

From the basin a long, steep, loose scree chute gains about 1,800 ft to Access Col at 6,100 ft, 2-3 hours, and it can be brutally hot with no shade. From the col, notoriously steep heather and talus lead to Luna Pass, where most parties camp near lingering snow patches for water.
hazards: A mile of genuine bushwhacking up Access Creek through devil's club, deadfall and huckleberry with biting insects
A long loose scree chute to Access Col with no shade
Notoriously steep heather between Access Col and Luna Pass; an axe is worthwhile on the short steep sections
Crevasses on the Southeast Glacier and a bergschrund near 7,900 ft
A final snowfield to nearly 50 degrees, with crampon-balling reported on wet snow
Wet, mossy rock on the lower of the two rib ledges

name: Northeast Buttress
approach: Southbound on the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT) down Bridge Creek, then northwest up North Fork Bridge Creek
descent: Descent is via the Southwest Couloir, downclimbed and rappelled from the summit ridge. The standard sequence is three rappels from the summit down along the ridge to Black Tooth Notch — the first rappel runs close to straight down the ridgeline, but the second and third are notably traversing (trending skier's right/rappeller's left), so there is real rope-snag risk and parties should watch their tails carefully. From the notch, simul-climb or scramble the connecting exposed 4th-class ledge, then make roughly three more single-rope rappels down into the SW couloir itself (six total is the commonly cited number, matching the route's historical rappel count; some parties link stations differently and report as few as five — e.g. two 30m rappels bridging the Black Tooth Notch section). A single 60m rope is sufficient for every station on this descent. Anchors are natural and fixed slings on horns/blocks rather than bolted stations, though they are described as 'well-established' — still, carry spare cord and rap rings to refresh sun-baked webbing. Below the raps, class 3 downclimbing continues down the couloir; where the gully narrows into cliffs lower down, exit left onto easier terrain and traverse back into the basin beneath the gully rather than rappelling the waterfall band. From the base of the couloir, descend scree/talus back to the Goode Glacier basin, re-cross the glacier, and reverse the approach down the North Fork Bridge Creek drainage to the PCT and trailhead — a long descent day that several parties report taking 8-10+ hours from summit to car, with real potential for benightment if the party is slow through the technical section.
hazards: rockfall
loose sections
crevasses on approach
long committing route
moat crossing and a steep (~50°) ice step where the route crosses onto the buttress toe from the Goode Glacier, worse late season
cornices possible on the approach in early season
difficult to retreat once high on the buttress — commit only with a stable weather window

waysIn.name: Bridge Creek and the North Fork to the moat below the red ledges
waysIn.season: Mid to late July through September. The moat crossing is easiest once the glacier has receded, around the third week of July, and gets harder again as the season goes on
waysIn.notes:
From the Bridge Creek / PCT trailhead off SR-20 near Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound about ten miles, losing steadily along Bridge Creek, to the North Fork Bridge Creek junction near North Fork Camp. Turn up the North Fork Bridge Creek trail and head upstream; it gets brushier and less maintained the further you go, with a log crossing at Grizzly Creek.

Around mile 13-14 the maintained tread effectively ends. Ford the North Fork — cold and sometimes knee deep, and easiest a few steps upstream at a cairn — then work up scree and third-class slabs on climber's right of the large waterfall draining toward the Goode Glacier, which is the way to avoid the worst brush. Look for the alder tunnel: a boot-path corridor through the slide alder that saves a great deal of thrashing.

Camp around the glacier toe at roughly 5,400-6,800 ft depending on how far you push. Plan on three to four days round trip.
hazards: A moat and bergschrund at the toe of the buttress with a steep step of about 50 degrees where the route steps off the Goode Glacier onto rock — worse as the season goes on, and reported by some parties as impassable late
Open crevasses and overhead serac hazard on the Goode Glacier
Loose and wet rock on the approach slabs beside the waterfall
Cornices on the approach in early season
A route that is difficult to retreat from once high on the buttress — commit only with a stable weather window
A descent by the Southwest Couloir that several parties report taking 8-10 hours from summit to car

name: Southeast Slope via Methow Pass
approach: From the PCT-Northbound (Rainy Pass) trailhead on SR 20 (elev. ~4,855-4,900 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail north. The trail climbs steadily through subalpine forest and larch parkland past Porcupine Creek, reaching Cutthroat Pass (6,820 ft) at about 4.9 miles / ~1,900 ft gain (roughly 2-2.5 hours at a hiking pace). There is no water at the pass itself; Porcupine Creek below is the last reliable source before the high country dries out in late summer, so top off there. From Cutthroat Pass continue north on the PCT, which drops to Granite Pass (~6,300 ft) and then contours across open, sparsely-treed slopes to Snowy Creek Meadow (~6,400-6,900 ft) - a common camp/water stop, with a short side-trail up to Snowy Lakes if you want a higher, more scenic bivy. From the meadow, stay on the PCT northbound roughly another 1-1.5 miles / ~350 ft gain (about an hour) to Methow Pass (~6,600 ft). Leave the trail here: travel west/southwest, off-trail, through open heather and talus benches toward Mount Hardy's east ridge. Gain the ridge and follow moderate slopes of sand, scree and talus - loose in spots, with real route-finding required - up to the saddle between the true summit and a lower false summit (roughly 7,200-7,600 ft). From the saddle, several hundred feet of enjoyable Class 2-3 scrambling over blocky rock leads to the summit at 8,097 ft; some parties note a notch below the true summit block that's crossed before a short, shallow summit gully. Total one-way distance from the trailhead to the summit is roughly 11-12 miles with about 5,100 ft of cumulative gain, matching the recorded figures - this is a long day for strong parties or, more commonly, a 2-day trip with camp near Snowy Creek Meadow/Snowy Lakes. Snow can linger on the upper ridge and in north-facing gullies near Cutthroat and Granite Passes well into early summer; the highway itself (and both this trailhead and the alternate Swamp Creek pullout used for the shorter South Ridge route) sit inside WSDOT's SR 20 winter closure zone, so the route is typically only accessible from around late April or May through November depending on snowpack. Carry an ice axe and know how to use it if attempting before the passes fully melt out.
descent: Descend the same line used on ascent: reverse the Class 2-3 scramble and scree/talus slopes back down to the saddle, then drop off the east ridge to Methow Pass and rejoin the PCT southbound. Retrace through Snowy Creek Meadow, Granite Pass, and Cutthroat Pass, then back down the PCT to the Rainy Pass trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb - no rappelling is involved on the standard route, so rappels = 0. In early season, lingering snow on the upper south-facing slopes below the saddle can sometimes be glissaded (ice axe and glissading skill required, and only where runouts are clean of rock); by mid-to-late summer this becomes a dry, loose scree/talus descent, so care with route-finding and loose rock is the main hazard, along with the long trail miles back to the car. Some parties returning from camp near Snowy Lakes cut cross-country along the open ridge back toward camp instead of the trail, but parties note this is scenic rather than faster, and it doesn't shorten the standard descent to the trailhead.
hazards: long, mostly off-trail approach via the PCT (Rainy Pass - Cutthroat Pass - Granite Pass - Methow Pass, then cross-country to the peak)
loose scree, talus, and blocky rock on the unmarked upper route, especially near the summit saddle and final gully
lingering snow and possible wet-slide/sluff activity on north-facing terrain and the Swamp Creek route's ~40-degree snow finger into early summer
cliff bands near 5,200 ft on the Swamp Creek approach ridge requiring correct routefinding (stay climber's right)
afternoon thunderstorms and rapid weather changes on the exposed ridge crest and passes
wildfire smoke can reduce visibility and air quality in late summer (Aug-Sept)

waysIn.name: Rainy Pass, the crest trail to Methow Pass, and the east ridge
waysIn.season: Late June through September, with July through September giving the driest scree. June ascents work but the final slopes and gully still hold snow and want an axe and crampons. The highway is shut for avalanche control through the winter, which closes both approaches outright.
waysIn.notes: The long way, and the one that suits a two-day trip. From the large paved lot on the north side of SR-20 at Rainy Pass, follow the crest trail north as it climbs steadily through subalpine forest and larch parkland past Porcupine Creek — fill up there, it is the last easy water before a long dry stretch of switchbacks — to Cutthroat Pass. From the pass the trail drops toward Granite Pass and a saddle beyond it, where a steep snowfield often lasts into August and has caused slide-for-life falls, so carry an axe if you are early in the season. Beyond, the trail contours across open, sparsely treed slopes to Snowy Creek Meadow, a common water and camp stop, with a short side trail west into the Snowy Lakes basin for a higher and more scenic bivy under Tower Mountain and Golden Horn. From the meadow, stay on the crest trail north to the open plateau at Methow Pass and leave it there: travel west and southwest off-trail through open heather and talus benches toward the peak's east ridge, gain the ridge, and follow moderate sand, scree and talus — loose in places, with real route-finding — up to the saddle between the true summit and its lower false summit.
hazards: Steep lingering snowfield just past Granite Pass that has caused slide-for-life falls into August
Long, mostly off-trail final leg from Methow Pass with no marked line
Loose scree, talus and blocky rock on the upper route, worst near the summit saddle and final gully
No water at Cutthroat Pass; Porcupine Creek is the last reliable source
Afternoon thunderstorms and fast weather changes on exposed ridge crest and passes
Wildfire smoke reducing visibility in late summer
Highway closure in winter cuts off road access entirely
waysIn.whyThisWay: For a two-day trip, or when linking Hardy with neighbours like Golden Horn or Holliway, using the crest trail instead of the steep day-trip slog from the Swamp Creek pullout.

waysIn.name: Swamp Creek pullout and the south ridge
waysIn.season: Late June through September once the snow finger has stabilised or melted, with July and August driest. Earlier in the season the finger is a snow climb rather than a scramble.
waysIn.notes: The short, steep alternative, and the way most day parties go. Start from the highway pullout at Swamp Creek and climb through brushy forest to the foot of the prominent ridge on the mountain's south side. Follow the ridge upward, staying on the crest where it lets you and moving climber's right to get around the cliff bands that block the crest around 5,200 ft — getting that traverse wrong is what turns parties back. Above the cliff bands the ridge opens out onto sand and scree and continues to the summit block. This side faces the sun and dries early, which is why it comes into condition before the crest-trail approach and why it turns into a loose, dusty grind by late summer; a snow finger on this flank can hold firm snow at a fairly steep angle into early summer, which speeds the ascent considerably for a party carrying an axe.
hazards: Cliff bands around 5,200 ft block the crest; bypass on climber's right is the main route-finding failure
Steep snow finger on this flank into early summer with wet-slide and sluff potential
Brushy forest on the lower ridge with no maintained tread
Loose scree and blocky rock on the upper route and in the final gully
Exposed ridge crest with no shelter from afternoon thunderstorms
Highway closure in winter cuts off road access entirely

name: Standard Scramble (South/East Slopes)
approach: Start from the Bagley Lakes Trailhead (~4,200 ft) at the south end of the upper Mt. Baker Ski Area parking lot near the Heather Meadows Visitor Center. Follow Bagley Lakes Trail (Forest Service Trail 684.1) south along the eastern shore of Bagley Lake — this is the only reliable water source on the route, and it should still be filtered/treated. At about 0.75 mile, the trail joins Chain Lakes Trail (Forest Service Trail 682), which bends west and begins switchbacking up toward Herman Saddle (~5,300 ft), roughly 1.5-2 miles and about 1,100 ft above the lakes. Snow frequently lingers on this slope into July or even August, and the Forest Service explicitly flags it as avalanche terrain in winter/spring conditions, so check current conditions before an early-season trip; poles and some route-finding are recommended even on the maintained tread. At the last switchback below Herman Saddle — the low point on the ridge connecting Mazama Dome (west) and Mount Herman (east) — leave the maintained trail and go cross-country, climbing open heather slopes and a short band of scrub trees for a couple hundred vertical feet to gain the Mazama Dome-Herman connecting ridge. This off-trail stretch is the route-finding crux of the approach; the correct exit point is easy to miss in poor visibility. Once on the ridge, follow its crest generally eastward, staying mostly on the south/southwest side over heather benches and loose scree/talus, to the base of a short final east ridge that leads to the true summit at 6,285 ft.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than any independent descent route. Downclimb the short summit east ridge back to the south/southwest ridge, then follow that ridge and its heather-and-scree slopes back down to the low saddle point between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman. Drop off the ridge on the same cross-country line through the scrub-tree band and heather slopes to rejoin the maintained Chain Lakes Trail (682) at the last switchback below Herman Saddle, then follow Chain Lakes Trail and Bagley Lakes Trail (684.1) back past Bagley Lakes to the trailhead. This is a walk-off scramble with no rappelling required under normal summer/dry conditions — 0 rappels. The main descent hazards are loose, down-sloping scree and talus on the ridge and connecting slopes (easy to kick rocks onto anyone below), and lingering snow in the gully/ridge-traverse sections in early season, where an ice axe and/or microspikes are a reasonable precaution; a rope is not standard gear for this route.
hazards: loose talus
lingering snow gullies
short exposed summit steps

waysIn.name: Bagley Lakes and Chain Lakes Trail to the last switchback below Herman Saddle, then cross-country to the ridge
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow lingers on the slope below Herman Saddle into July or August and the Forest Service flags it as avalanche terrain in winter and spring
waysIn.notes:
Start at the Bagley Lakes Trailhead around 4,200 ft, at the south end of the upper Mount Baker Ski Area parking lot near the Heather Meadows Visitor Center. Follow Bagley Lakes Trail #684.1 south along the east shore of Bagley Lake — the only reliable water on the route, and it should still be treated.

At about three quarters of a mile the trail joins Chain Lakes Trail #682, which bends west and switchbacks up toward Herman Saddle at roughly 5,300 ft, about 1.5-2 miles and 1,100 ft above the lakes.

At the last switchback below Herman Saddle, leave the maintained trail and climb open heather and a short band of scrub trees for a couple of hundred vertical feet to gain the connecting ridge between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman.

Then follow the crest generally east, staying mostly on the south and southwest side over heather benches and loose scree and talus, to the base of a short final east ridge.
hazards: An unmarked exit at the last switchback below the saddle, easy to miss in poor visibility
Lingering snow on the Chain Lakes switchbacks into July or August, flagged as avalanche terrain in winter and spring
Loose down-sloping scree and talus on the connecting ridge, easy to kick onto anyone below
Only one water source, at Bagley Lake, and it needs treating
Two summits on one ridge — Mazama Dome west, Herman east

name: Hinman Glacier / Standard
approach: Park at the Necklace Valley Trailhead (~1,650 ft) at the end of FR 68 and start up Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first ~5 miles are deceptively easy, gaining only about 600 ft as the trail follows the East Fork Foss River through regenerated second-growth forest (logged in the 1930s), entering the Alpine Lakes Wilderness at about 1.5 miles. Around the 5-mile mark the trail crosses the East Fork Foss River on a footlog with a handwire (the river runs high and cold under it in early-season snowmelt, so plan the crossing for morning low flow) and then turns uphill in earnest, climbing roughly 2,400 ft over the next 3 miles on steep, root-laced switchbacks into Necklace Valley proper. This section is the approach's real crux for tired legs and pack weight. The trail eases again as it reaches Jade Lake (~4,600 ft, ~8-9 miles), then Emerald Lake a quarter mile beyond, then Opal Lake, threading through the swampy, lake-studded Necklace Basin — good camping and reliable water throughout, but buggy in early/mid-summer. From the head of Necklace Basin the maintained trail ends; continue cross-country (an established, cairned climbers' path through meadow and boulder talus) up and southeast roughly 1-1.5 miles and ~1,000+ ft to La Bohn Gap and the La Bohn Lakes, the standard high camp for the peak (total approach to La Bohn Gap is about 10-11 miles one-way with ~5,000+ ft of cumulative gain). From La Bohn Gap the route continues north-northeast into what remains of the Hinman/Foss Glacier basin — now much diminished and largely bare rock/permanent snowfield rather than a true crevassed glacier in most recent seasons, but still worth crampons/axe and glacier-travel judgment in early season or after a big snow year — then east/east-northeast via easy class 2 ridge/scree scrambling to the summit ridge and along it about half a mile to the true summit (7,492 ft). Loose rock on the final scramble and potential crevasse/bergschrund hazard on the lingering glacier remnant (mostly early-season) are the main approach-specific risks beyond the river crossing and the steep valley headwall.
descent: This is a walk-off / downclimb descent with no rappelling — reverse the ascent line the entire way. From the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 ridge scramble back to the top of the glacier remnant, descend the snow/glacier basin back to La Bohn Gap (watch for softened, sun-cupped snow and any residual crevasse slots in early season), then follow the cairned climbers' path back down through the talus and meadow to La Bohn Lakes/Necklace Basin. Most parties treat this as a multi-day trip (roundtrip totals run 22-26 miles with 5,700-9,000 ft of cumulative gain/loss depending on exact line), descending from the summit back to a La Bohn Lakes or Necklace Basin camp the same day and hiking the remaining ~9-10 miles out to the trailhead — back down through Necklace Basin past Opal, Emerald, and Jade Lakes, down the steep rooty 2,400-ft headwall, back across the East Fork Foss River footlog, and out the long, gentle lower trail — on a subsequent day. No technical rope work is required on the standard route; the notable descent hazards are the same river crossing, loose talus, and glacier-remnant travel encountered on the way in, now tackled with tired legs late in the day.
