hazards: Hinman Glacier is functionally gone — declared dead (non-flowing) in 2022 and reduced to a few stagnant ice/snow patches; expect unstable talus and loose blocks the size of dining tables on slopes that used to be glacier-covered, not a crevassed glacier crossing
remnant blue-ice patches can still demand crampons even though roped glacier travel/crevasse rescue gear is no longer typically needed
long, remote approach (roughly 18-25 mile round trip depending on route/side trips) with no cell coverage and a realistic 2-3 day commitment
route-finding on the broad, complex summit ridge — the true summit is a jagged rock outcrop at the east end of the ridge, easy to mistake for a false high point from a distance

waysIn.name: Necklace Valley to La Bohn Gap and the lakes
waysIn.season: July to September. Most parties make it a two or three day trip
waysIn.notes:
Park at the Necklace Valley trailhead at about 1,650 ft at the end of FR 68 and start up Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first five miles are deceptively flat, gaining only about 600 ft along the East Fork Foss River, entering the wilderness at about 1.5 miles.

Around mile 5 the trail crosses the East Fork Foss River on a footlog with a handwire; the river runs high and cold under it in early-season melt, so cross in the morning at low flow. Then it turns uphill in earnest, roughly 2,400 ft over three miles of steep, root-laced switchbacks. This is the real crux of the approach for tired legs.

The grade eases at Jade Lake at about 4,600 ft and eight to nine miles, then Emerald and Opal Lakes through the swampy Necklace Basin — good camping and reliable water, buggy in early summer.

From the head of Necklace Basin the maintained trail ends. Continue cross-country on an established, cairned climbers' path through meadow and boulder talus, up and southeast roughly a mile to a mile and a half and over 1,000 ft, to La Bohn Gap and the La Bohn Lakes. That is the standard high camp: about 10 to 11 miles one way with over 5,000 ft of cumulative gain.
hazards: An unbridged ford of the East Fork Foss River around mile 5, high and cold in early-season melt
2,400 ft of steep root-laced switchbacks with a multi-day pack
Crevasse and bergschrund hazard on the lingering glacier remnant, mostly early season
Loose rock on the final class 2 scramble
Mosquitoes in the lake basins in early and mid summer
A long walk out from a remote camp if anything goes wrong

name: Southeast Route
approach: Park at the Necklace Valley (East Fork Foss) trailhead at the end of FR 68 and follow the East Fork Foss trail up the valley. The first five miles are gentle forest, gaining only about 600 ft, until a footlog crossing of the East Fork Foss River, then the trail climbs about 2,400 ft in three miles of steep, rooty switchbacks to Jade Lake and on up the Necklace Valley past the other lakes. Leave the valley trail at its upper end, where the hanging valley leads to La Bohn Lakes and the climb proper. Camps at the lakes or in Necklace Valley make this a two-day trip for most parties. From the end of the valley, climb the boulder gully or the waterfall route to La Bohn Gap (about 6,000 ft); the snow chute is the early-season option and needs an axe. The route starts from the gap, where a clear climbers' boot track turns north.
descent: Reverse the ridge and boot track to La Bohn Gap, downclimbing the class 2 to 3 rock, which is loose throughout. From the gap descend to the valley floor by the boulder gully, by the waterfall route beside it, or by the snow chute when it is soft; hard early-season snow calls for an axe and crampons. Then follow Necklace Valley trail past the lakes, down the steep 2,400 ft switchbacks to the footlog across the East Fork Foss River, and out the five gentle miles to the trailhead.

name: West Ridge
approach: Park at the Necklace Valley (East Fork Foss) trailhead at the end of FR 68 and follow the East Fork Foss trail up the valley. The first five miles are gentle forest, gaining only about 600 ft, until a footlog crossing of the East Fork Foss River, then the trail climbs about 2,400 ft in three miles of steep, rooty switchbacks to Jade Lake and on up the Necklace Valley past the other lakes. Leave the valley trail at its upper end, where the hanging valley leads to La Bohn Lakes and the climb proper. Camps at the lakes or in Necklace Valley make this a two-day trip for most parties. From the end of the valley, hug the tree line left, following cairns up heather to the outlet of the lower La Bohn Lake, then continue to the upper lake; the ridge above it is the start of the climb.
descent: Reverse the ridge to La Bohn Lakes. The rock on the ridge is loose, with blocks that shift underfoot, so test holds and keep clear of other parties. From the lakes, drop back to Necklace Valley either by the heather and cairn line along the tree line or by the boulder gully and stream below La Bohn Gap, which is mostly class 2; in early season the snow chute to the gap needs an ice axe and often crampons. Then follow Necklace Valley trail down past the lakes, the steep 2,400 ft switchbacks and the footlog, and out the flat five miles to the trailhead.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: The North Fork Skokomish Trail from Staircase to First Divide and the Home Sweet Home Trail from First Divide down to the Duckabush have been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date; check the park's trail conditions before planning. When open, the standard way in starts at the Staircase trailhead (~785 ft) and follows the North Fork Skokomish River Trail up the valley through old-growth forest, past Camp Pleasant to Nine Stream Camp, where the trail fords the river (deep and swift in high snowmelt or heavy rain). Above Nine Stream it climbs steeply past Two Bear Camp, brushy between Two Bear and the divide, to First Divide (4,688 ft), about 12.5 miles from the trailhead. The much longer alternative comes up the Duckabush River Trail and climbs over First Divide from the north past Home Sweet Home. Just below First Divide on the Skokomish side, the long-abandoned Mount Hopper Way leaves the main trail; its tread has gone under brush, so expect to bushwhack south and east through forest, then climb open talus and subalpine meadow toward Mount Hopper's basin below the summit rockwall (high point ~6,120 ft). This upper stretch has real route-finding difficulty: numerous gullies and ribs look equally plausible from below, snow can choke the gully well into summer (ice axe advisable), and the final scramble features loose rock underfoot — expect to backtrack if you pick the wrong line. Most parties make it a multi-day trip, camping at Two Bear Camp, First Divide or Home Sweet Home rather than pushing car-to-car.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the same gully/rib system off the summit rockwall back down through the steepest rock step, then the easier talus and heather below it, back to the basin and First Divide (4,688 ft). This is a scramble route with no fixed anchors or bolted stations reported anywhere on it — the standard descent is careful downclimbing, facing in through the steeper rocky steps near the top where the wall lays back into a short climbable face. Some parties uncomfortable reversing that headwall step opt for a single, short rappel off a natural anchor (slung horn or block — bring webbing/cord, since none is fixed in place) to protect the crux; this is optional, not required, so plan on 0 fixed rappels for a typical descent. Watch for loose rock and rockfall onto any party below in the gully system, and re-identify your ascent gully carefully from above — the same routefinding hazard (many similar-looking gullies and ribs) applies in reverse and is arguably worse on the way down. From First Divide, reverse the North Fork Skokomish Trail about 12.5 miles to Staircase (or, if you came in from the Duckabush, drop past Home Sweet Home to the Duckabush River Trail and walk it out). Both trails off First Divide, the Home Sweet Home Trail toward the Duckabush and the North Fork Skokomish Trail to Staircase, are currently closed after the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire; check the park's trail status before planning.
hazards: Loose talus and meadow slopes on the upper mountain
Steep snow on the approach into early summer
Very long, remote wilderness approach far from help
Rockfall, treefall, and landslide hazard in the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire burn scar along the closed Staircase approach corridor
Largely off-trail, unbridged travel on the longer Duckabush/Marmot Lake alternate approach

waysIn.name: First Divide from the Duckabush and Marmot Lake
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: The historic Skokomish approach is closed by fire damage, and so is this one where it leaves the Duckabush: the park lists the Home Sweet Home Trail, from the Duckabush River Trail junction over First Divide, closed for the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire with no reopening date (trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026), so no open trail reaches First Divide while the closure stands. When it reopens, the way in is the long Duckabush valley over Big Hump to Marmot Lake, then back to the Home Sweet Home junction and over First Divide. Roughly double the old distance and firmly a multi-day trip with a camp at the lake or at Home Sweet Home.
hazards: Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, no reopening date
Long Duckabush valley approach, largely off-trail and unbridged on the Marmot Lake alternate
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall along the closed corridor
Many similar gullies and ribs below the summit rockwall; wrong lines wall up
Snow choking the summit gully well into summer; ice axe advisable
Loose talus and steep meadow slopes on the upper mountain
Rockfall onto anyone below in the gully system
Very long, remote walk-out far from help
waysIn.whyThisWay: When coming from the Duckabush side as a longer multi-day trip with a night at Marmot Lake, once the closed trail to First Divide reopens.

waysIn.name: Staircase and the North Fork Skokomish to First Divide
waysIn.notes: The historic and shortest way in. From Staircase, follow the North Fork Skokomish trail up the valley to Home Sweet Home and on to First Divide, where the scramble leaves the trail. Fire damage has affected this corridor, so check the park's trail status before planning.
hazards: North Fork Skokomish Trail closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, no reopening date
Rockfall, treefall and landslide hazard in the burn scar along the Staircase corridor
Deep, swift ford of the river at Nine Stream Camp in high snowmelt or heavy rain
Brushy, steep trail between Two Bear Camp and First Divide; abandoned Hopper Way tread lost under brush
Many similar gullies and ribs below the summit rockwall; wrong lines wall up
Snow on the approach and in the summit gully into early summer
Loose talus and steep meadow slopes on the upper mountain
Very long, remote wilderness approach far from help

name: South Slope
approach: Two common trailheads on US-2 in Chelan County give access. Merritt Lake Trailhead (3,000 ft, high-clearance/AWD recommended on the access road): from Leavenworth take US-2 west about 24 miles (or from Stevens Pass, east about 11.5 miles) to milepost 76, turn onto Forest Road 657, and continue 1.5 miles to the trailhead; hike the Merritt Lake Trail (2,000 ft gain in 2.5 miles) then join the Nason Ridge Trail east to Crescent Lake. Rock Mountain Trailhead (2,650-2,675 ft, no fee): on US-2 near milepost 73, about 27 miles west of Leavenworth / 8.5 miles east of Stevens Pass; follow the Rock Mountain Trail up to Rock Lake (snow persists above ~5,000 ft into late spring), then over the Rock-Crescent col and down about 500 ft to Crescent Lake. From either approach, water is available at Crescent Lake but is unreliable higher on the mountain.
descent: Downclimb the loose class 3 gully on the upper south face with care — it is dirty and holds are unreliable in both directions. Below that, descend talus and open slopes back to Crescent Lake. In early-season (spring) conditions the col/gully snow can refreeze firm overnight, making crampons and an ice axe useful for a controlled descent; some parties glissade snow-filled sections when soft. From Crescent Lake, retrace the Nason Ridge Trail to the trailhead, watching for the correct drainage — parties have mistakenly dropped toward Royal Creek from the ridge.
hazards: Significant off-trail talus and brush travel requiring real routefinding skill
Loose rock in the upper south-face gully
Seasonal cornice/wind-slab and slough hazard on the approach col into the Crescent Lake basin
Remote National Forest backcountry with no confirmed cell coverage

waysIn.name: Merritt Lake Trailhead and Nason Ridge Trail to Crescent Lake
waysIn.season: July into October once the ridge clears; snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring.
waysIn.notes: The shorter and more direct way in. From the highway turn onto the rough forest road — high clearance is worth having — and drive to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. Climb the Merritt Lake trail to the lake, then join the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it east to Crescent Lake, which sits below the peak's south side. Water is available at Crescent Lake but is unreliable higher on the mountain, so fill there. The trail is well defined the whole way to the lake, and everything above it is your own route-finding.
hazards: Wrong-drainage risk: several small bowls resemble the south face and one is the Royal Creek drainage
Boot path leaving the ridge trail northward leads to the neighbouring summit, not this one
No established route above Crescent Lake; route-finding is entirely your own
Loose, dirty Class 3 gully through the cliff band, unreliable holds in both directions
Off-trail talus and brush with slippery grass and dense alder low on the face
Water unreliable above Crescent Lake; remote, no confirmed cell coverage

waysIn.name: Rock Mountain Trailhead via Rock Lake and the Rock–Crescent col
waysIn.season: July into October. Snow lingers above about 5,000 ft into late spring and the col holds it longest.
waysIn.notes: The longer and more scenic way in, and the one commonly used by parties who want the neighbouring summit in the same outing. From the highway near the milepost, climb the Rock Mountain trail to Rock Lake — snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring on this side — then cross the col between the two peaks and descend roughly five hundred feet on the far side to Crescent Lake. From there the climb is the same as from the other trailhead. It costs a substantial descent that has to be regained on the return, which is the price of the extra ground it covers.
hazards: About 500 ft descent from the Rock-Crescent col to Crescent Lake that must be regained on the way out
Snow persisting on the col and above ~5,000 ft on Rock Lake side into late spring
Wrong-drainage risk: several small bowls resemble the south face
Loose, dirty Class 3 gullies through the cliff band above the lake
Off-trail talus and brush above the lake; remote, no confirmed cell coverage
Long day made longer by the added distance; water unreliable above Crescent Lake
waysIn.whyThisWay: When also climbing Rock Mountain, running a car-shuttle traverse, or when the rough road to Merritt Lake is impassable; longer, with a descent to Crescent Lake that must be regained.

name: North Face (North Peak)
approach: Lake Serene Trail (#1068) from the Mount Index Road trailhead, 3.6 miles / roughly 1,920 ft gain to Lake Serene (about 1.5-2 hours), then talus and grass slopes on the west side of the lake (near an old rockslide) to reach the base of the North Peak's broken, bushy lower spur.
descent: Reported round-trip climbing time is roughly 6-8 hours up and about 5 hours down from the base, on loose terrain that demands careful downclimbing/rappelling through the brushy, broken lower rib. Rappel anchors near the summit have been refreshed, and in mid-June they formed a clear path down the descent.
hazards: Loose, sometimes rotten rock throughout much of the route
Long, complex descent through brushy, broken terrain
Historic ambiguity over whether the 1929 first-ascent party actually reached the true summit

waysIn.name: Lake Serene Trail #1068 to the north side of North Peak
waysIn.season: Jun-Sep, after several consecutive dry days
waysIn.notes:
From US-2 at milepost 35.2 turn south on Mount Index Road and drive 0.3 miles to the Lake Serene trailhead at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs roughly 3.6 to 4.1 miles and about 2,000 ft to the lake at around 2,500 ft, passing the Bridal Veil Falls spur near mile 1.6. The maintained trail ends at the lake's north end.

From there, traverse talus and very large boulders along the west and south side of the lake, near an old rockslide, toward the base of North Peak's wall. In early season this crossing goes over avalanche debris and snow and ice piled at the water's edge.
hazards: Wet moss on downsloping slabs — low-angle ground that is genuinely serious
Avalanche debris and lingering snow at the lake edge in early season
Vertical brush steps with no protection
Loose, vegetated rock throughout; slow retreat

name: Standard Route
approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, start on Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 through second-growth and then old-growth forest along the Dungeness River. At about 1 mile, bear right at the signed junction onto the Royal Basin Trail (the left fork continues up-valley toward Boulder Shelter/Constance Pass). The Royal Basin trail then climbs gradually for several miles alongside Royal Creek — the main water source for the approach — crossing it on log/plank bridges more than once; these crossings can run fast and cold during early-season snowmelt (June). Around mile 6 the grade steepens sharply for the push to Royal Lake (7.2 mi, roughly 2,500 ft gained from the trailhead), with the final mile gaining about 500 ft on looser, sometimes-eroded tread. From Royal Lake continue south up-valley on the scramblers'/climbers' path roughly another 0.8 mile and 600 ft to Upper Royal Basin (about 8 mi in, ~5,700 ft), a broad heather-and-tarn basin below Mount Deception's northeast face that most parties use as base camp (NPS wilderness permit and bear canister required; no fires; advance reservations cover June 15–Oct 15). From Upper Royal Basin the maintained trail ends; head cross-country west up heather benches and talus to the rim of the glacial moraine ringing Surprise Basin, the small hanging cirque between Mount Martin, Mount Johnson, and Mount Clark. Drop into Surprise Basin and cross its snowfields (crampons/axe often useful into July) toward the roughly 6,900 ft notch/col between Johnson (climber's left) and Clark (climber's right) — this is the standard gateway to Johnson's upper mountain. This off-trail stretch above Upper Royal Basin is loose talus and scree with genuine rockfall and route-finding hazard; helmets on from the moraine rim upward. Given the total distance (~19 miles / 30.9 km round trip) and elevation gain, most parties backpack in and camp at Upper Royal Basin, climbing Johnson as a long day from camp rather than attempting it car-to-car. Past the upper Royal Basin tarn, cross a small ridge west into Surprise Basin; in early September the glacier there had melted back to a deep blue lake, and from its shore the notch between Clark and Johnson is in direct view.
descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb from the summit back to the ~6,900 ft Johnson–Clark notch, then retrace the talus-and-moraine descent down into Surprise Basin and back over its rim to Upper Royal Basin, from which the Royal Basin/Upper Dungeness Trail leads back out to the trailhead. The class 4 terrain near the summit is the crux of the descent as well as the ascent — the rock is loose enough in spots that most reported difficulty on this peak comes from downclimbing it, so face in and test holds on anything above class 3. The summit chimney is downclimbed rather than rappelled; there are no fixed/bolted rappel stations reported on Johnson, so a party that wants a rope on the steepest step, particularly if the rock is wet, must rig it from a natural anchor (horn, chockstone, or slung block) of its own. The summit block has a solid class 4 crack for the direct finish, plus a cairned class 3 bypass that is the gentler way to come down.
hazards: loose rock on the upper mountain
exposure on summit approach
very long interior approach (14+ miles round trip and 2,500+ ft of gain just to reach Royal Basin, adding significant commitment and complicating self-rescue)
remnant glacier/permanent snowfield crossing below the Clark-Johnson col (carry an ice axe, especially early season)
route-finding trap above the upper snowfield: exiting too far right leads into steepening gullies under the spires that are hard to reverse

waysIn.name: Royal Basin and Surprise Basin to the Clark–Johnson col
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: About seven miles to Royal Lake with the last mile eroded and loose, then most of another to the broad heather-and-tarn basin used as base camp. Above that the trail ends: heather benches and talus to the moraine rim, down into Surprise Basin, and across its snowfields to the col. Helmets on from the rim upward — the talus above is loose enough to matter.
hazards: Consistently loose and rotten rock, worst in the upper sections
Class 4 downclimbing that is harder than the same ground going up
Snowfield crossing below the col — axe useful into July
Gullies under Sweat Spire and Gasp Pinnacle that steepen into rounded steps if you leave the upper snowfield too far right
A long interior approach that complicates any self-rescue

name: Mount La Crosse Scramble
approach: From US 101 near Brinnon, take Duckabush River Road (FR 2510) west — paved for the first 3.6 miles, then gravel for a total of about 6 miles — to the Duckabush trailhead (FR 2510-060). Follow the Duckabush River Trail up the valley about 16.7 miles to the La Crosse Pass Trail junction (~2,650 ft), then climb the La Crosse Pass Trail north, about 3 miles and 2,900 ft of steep switchbacks, to La Crosse Pass (5,566 ft). Leave the trail at the pass for the off-trail Class 2-3 scramble west along the ridge to the summit.
descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling. Reverse the ridge and talus scramble back down to LaCrosse Pass, picking your way carefully back through the loose Class 2–3 terrain (descending loose talus is where most of the slip-and-slide hazard on this route actually lives, more than on the ascent). From the pass, descend the LaCrosse Pass Trail to whichever trailhead your itinerary uses. If you're headed out the Duckabush side, be ready for a knee-punishing, steep, switchbacking drop of about 3,000 ft in roughly a mile back to the Duckabush River Trail junction — this section is loose underfoot and eroded in spots, and is meaningfully harder on tired legs descending than it is climbing. If you're exiting north toward the Dosewallips/West Fork Dosewallips, the grade down from the pass is gentler and more forgiving. In poor visibility, the open, sparsely-cairned country right around the pass and upper basin is the spot most likely to cause route-finding trouble on the way down — many parties mention losing the tread in lingering snowfields near the pass well into early summer. Rather than retrace the crest, a lower traverse back toward the pass is possible, but it crosses a deep washout gully on the sub-summit's face and is just as slow (July).
hazards: No water at La Crosse Pass — carry in from a lower creek crossing
Off-trail cross-country travel above the pass; easy to lose the route in fog without map/compass or GPS
Lingering snow on north-facing slopes/gullies into early July, requiring ice axe/traction in early season
Black bears in the LaCrosse Basin — bear canisters required
Very long, remote approach with no cell coverage — self-rescue distance is measured in days

waysIn.name: Duckabush River Trail to La Crosse Pass
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: A long valley walk to the La Crosse Pass junction, then a steep switchbacking climb of roughly three thousand feet in about a mile to the pass — loose and eroded in places and considerably harder coming down on tired legs. The West Fork Dosewallips reaches the same pass on a gentler grade and is the kinder exit if you are through-hiking.
hazards: No water at the pass or above it — carry from a creek far below
Open, sparsely cairned country that is easy to lose in fog
Snow on north-facing slopes and gullies into early July
Loose talus that is more hazardous descending than climbing
Bear canisters required and a self-rescue distance measured in days

name: South Slope - South Face (Standard Route)
approach: From the Robinson Creek Trailhead (~2,500 ft, via SR-20 and Lost River Road/Forest Road 5400 west of Winthrop), follow the Robinson Creek/Middle Fork Pasayten Trail over Robinson Pass and down into the Middle Fork Pasayten drainage. Continue north down the valley past the first Eureka Creek Trail junction and, about 4.8 miles beyond the Whistler Cutoff, turn east on the Eureka Creek Trail up Berk Creek to Fred's Lake (6,507 ft), a common camp and water source below Lago's west side. From Fred's Lake, follow the unmaintained middle section of the Eureka Creek Trail (or cross-country) east across the upper Eureka Creek basin - the creek crossing can be difficult when swollen with snowmelt - to reach Shellrock Basin/Shellrock Pass on the south side of the Lago-Carru ridge. The shortest road-based approach is roughly 16 miles one-way, typically covered over 1-2 days.
descent: From the summit, descend the loose South Slope/South Face talus and scree, or drop via the Southwest Slope variant, which avoids some of the steeper upper rock ribs. Many parties traverse instead to the Lago-Carru col to tag Mount Carru before returning to camp rather than descending fully and re-climbing. The rock is loose throughout, so move carefully, stay spread out, and watch for parties below.
hazards: The upper mountain is composed of notoriously loose, crumbly rock requiring careful, deliberate movement throughout the ascent.
This is grizzly and black bear country near the Canadian border; proper food storage is essential.
Long stretches of open talus and ridge above treeline offer no protection from sudden thunderstorms.

waysIn.name: From Robinson Creek over Robinson Pass
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Lago is the highest peak in this group and the least loved underfoot, being a large pile of loose rock where the whole ascent asks for deliberate movement rather than any technique. Camp is normally Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin, reached along the Middle Fork Pasayten, either over Robinson Pass from the low Robinson Creek trailhead or down the Whistler Cutoff from the high start at Slate Pass, with an awkward crossing of upper Eureka Creek when it is swollen with snowmelt. From camp the round trip is a half day. Many parties link straight over to Carru by the connecting col rather than descending and re-climbing, and the southwest slope is a common variation for coming down since it avoids some of the steeper upper rock ribs.
hazards: Notoriously loose, crumbly rock throughout the upper mountain; rockfall onto parties stacked below
Enormous cliff on the north side of the summit ridge
Difficult crossing of upper Eureka Creek when swollen with snowmelt
Open talus and crest give no shelter from thunderstorms
Unmarked cross-country travel; lingering early-season snow in couloirs
Grizzly and black bear country; food storage required
waysIn.whyThisWay: When starting from the low Robinson Creek trailhead instead of the high start at Slate Pass; a much longer walk that reaches the same Pasayten camps.

waysIn.name: From Slate Pass down the Middle Fork Pasayten
waysIn.notes: The high start most parties use. From Slate Pass the trail drops north into the Middle Fork Pasayten; follow it down-valley past the Berk Creek junction, then climb to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin to camp. Lago is usually combined with Carru and Osceola.
hazards: Notoriously loose, crumbly rock throughout the upper mountain; rockfall onto parties below
Enormous cliff on the north side of the summit ridge
Awkward crossing of upper Eureka Creek when swollen with snowmelt on the way to camp
Long walk down the Middle Fork Pasayten then back up to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin
Open talus and crest give no shelter from thunderstorms; grizzly and black bear country
Unmarked cross-country travel; lingering early-season snow

name: South Ridge
approach: Park at the Twin Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS-3065 (the last 2 miles are rough, high-clearance terrain — many parties park lower and walk the road). From the trailhead, follow the Winchester Mountain Trail (#685) briefly; at about 0.5 mile a signed junction splits left to Winchester Lookout and right onto the High Pass Trail (#676) — take the right fork. High Pass Trail #676 climbs through meadows and crosses an avalanche chute beneath Winchester Mountain (steep, exposed snowfields can linger here into August — an ice axe and snow-travel experience are recommended until the chute melts out), then continues up over Low Pass and on to High Pass, passing the old tailings and remains of the historic Gargett Mine just below the pass. High Pass is reached roughly 2 miles / 1.5–2 hours from the trailhead and makes a scenic, if exposed, campsite. There is no reliable water past this point in late season, so treat/carry water from Twin Lakes or early snowmelt. Beyond High Pass the maintained trail ends; an unmarked climbers' path continues west, contouring and dropping 100–200 ft into the basin below Larrabee's south face (around 6,400 ft you pass a small cliff band). Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, up to the southwest spur at approximately 6,900 ft. Here the route-finding crux: locate a gully system cut into the rock face — of two narrow parallel channels about 30 feet apart, take the right-hand one. Ascend the narrowing gully, which opens into broken rock, to gain the crest of the south ridge. Follow the ridge crest, favoring the west side, to the summit; a faint boot path and scattered cairns mark much of this stretch but both disappear for long sections, so be prepared to route-find. Total distance is roughly 8–10 miles round trip with on the order of 3,500–4,000 ft of cumulative elevation gain (the up-and-over via Low Pass and High Pass adds real gain beyond straight-line distance to the summit). The rock throughout — especially the gully and upper ridge — is notoriously loose and crumbly by Cascades standards; helmets are strongly recommended and parties should keep group size small (6 or fewer) and spread out to manage rockfall risk to those below.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line — there is no technical descent gear needed and this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route. From the summit, follow the ridge crest (favoring the west side) back down to where you gained it, then descend the gully system, taking the same right-hand channel used on the way up; this loose, narrow gully is the most hazard-prone part of the descent (parties frequently trigger rockfall here even while descending carefully — down-climb one at a time or spread well apart, and keep helmets on). Below the gully, cross the broken rock and scree back down to the southwest spur (~6,900 ft) and continue down through the boulder fields and basin to regain the climbers' path near High Pass, watching for the intermittent cairns since the way trail vanishes in spots. From High Pass, retrace the High Pass Trail (#676) back over Low Pass, across the avalanche chute below Winchester Mountain (glissading or plunge-stepping lingering snow here can save time in early/mid season, but stay alert to runout hazard), and down the Winchester Mountain Trail (#685) to the Twin Lakes Trailhead.
hazards: Loose, crumbly phyllite/greenstone rock throughout the gully and upper ridge — frequent rockfall
Steep, often corniced snow-filled summit gully lingers into July
Easy to mistakenly follow a boot path toward the East Ridge instead of the correct South/SW line

waysIn.name: Twin Lakes, High Pass Trail #676 over Low Pass, then the basin to the southwest spur
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep at best; snow lingers in the gully into August and in the avalanche chute below Winchester
waysIn.notes:
Park at the Twin Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS-3065; the last two miles are rough and many parties park lower and walk the road. From the trailhead follow Winchester Mountain Trail #685 briefly; at about half a mile a signed junction splits left to the Winchester lookout and right onto High Pass Trail #676. Take the right fork.

#676 climbs through meadows and crosses an avalanche chute beneath Winchester Mountain, where steep exposed snowfields can linger into August, then goes over Low Pass and on to High Pass, passing the tailings and remains of the historic Gargett Mine just below the pass. High Pass is roughly two miles and an hour and a half to two hours from the trailhead. There is no reliable water past this point late season.

Beyond High Pass the maintained trail ends. An unmarked climbers' path continues west, contouring and dropping 100-200 ft into the basin below Larrabee's south face, passing a small cliff band around 6,400 ft. Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, up to the southwest spur at about 6,900 ft.

Keep the party to six or fewer and spread out. The rock here is notoriously loose even by Cascades standards.
hazards: Two nearly identical parallel gullies thirty feet apart, only one of which is the route
Notoriously loose and crumbly rock in the gully and on the upper ridge — helmets, small parties, spread out
An avalanche chute below Winchester Mountain holding steep snow into August
A faint boot path and cairns that disappear for long sections above the gully
No reliable water past High Pass late season

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Via the North Fork Quinault Trailhead (North Shore Road), hike the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream past Elip Creek and Trapper Shelter until you are below Lawson's steep north flanks, which come into view approaching Twelve Mile flat — the fords at Wild Rose Creek and Elip Creek can be difficult or impassable in high water — then ford the North Fork and leave the trail, climbing off-trail directly up Lawson's north side.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly: down the North Ridge to the top of the chute, then down-climb the loose chute back to the valley floor — this is the most hazard-prone part of the descent, since the same scree and rockbands that were merely tedious going up become genuinely slippery and rockfall-prone with tired legs and no rope; move one at a time through any narrows and stay alert for parties below. At the bottom, re-ford the North Fork Quinault River (same knee-to-thigh-deep crossing as the approach — check levels, as afternoon snowmelt can raise it) to regain the maintained trail, then simply walk the North Fork Quinault River Trail back out to the trailhead, re-fording Elip and Wild Rose Creeks en route. There is no rappelling on this route: it is a scramble/walk-off (Grade I, Class 3 via the North Ridge, 'Basic Snow/Rock Scramble', or Class 2 hiking), and nothing on it involves fixed anchors, bolts, or rope work — a hand line could be a reasonable precaution for a mixed-experience party on the loose upper chute or on lingering early-season snow, but it is not a technical necessity.
hazards: routefinding on trail-less terrain
afternoon weather
difficult fords at Wild Rose Creek, Elip Creek, and the North Fork Quinault itself at Sixteen Mile Camp

name: North Ridge from Flapjack Lakes
approach: Approach via the Staircase / North Fork Skokomish trail (7.5 mi to Flapjack Lakes, ~3,100 ft gain) to Flapjack Lakes, then off-trail into the Sawtooth Ridge to the base of the climbing. Usually an overnight trip. Both the North Fork Skokomish River Trail beyond the Staircase Rapids Loop and the Flapjack Lakes Trail have been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire. The Staircase road and campground reopened on July 8, 2026, but no reopening date had been announced for the trails as of September 2026, so confirm with Olympic National Park that the trail (not just the Staircase road and campground) is open before planning a trip. A largely abandoned alternate line follows an old trail up the south end of Sawtooth Ridge, starting about 2.4 miles up the Staircase/North Fork Skokomish trail; it has been in poor condition and rarely used since the 1985 Beaver Fire.
descent: Most parties reverse the ascent line rather than descending a different route. Downclimb off the summit block through the gully system back to the Sawtooth Ridge crest, then drop off its west side by a steep gully (dirt first, then scree, talus and boulders) into the forest and work back through the brush to Flapjack Lakes. From there it's a long but straightforward hike down the Flapjack Lakes Trail / North Fork Skokomish River Trail to Staircase. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no fixed rappel stations, bolted anchors, or documented rope-descent points were found for the standard scramble route, so rappels = 0. The crux is reversing the airy class 3+ (occasional class-4-feeling move) terrain right off the summit block and negotiating chockstones/ledges partway down the gully; a short handline for less-experienced party members on this section is a reasonable precaution some parties use, but it is not a technical anchor-and-rope rappel. Primary descent hazards: route-finding (several similar-looking gully systems seam the south face — parties have reported descending the wrong chute/chockstone gully and encountering sketchy downclimbing before regaining the correct line or Madeline Creek drainage), loose rock/choss on the ridge and gully walls, and lingering snow in the descent gully into midsummer (ice axe useful into July). Plan for a long day — trip reports commonly cite 11–14+ hours car-to-car — and carry a headlamp and extra water for the trail miles back to Staircase.
hazards: Loose rock and scree on sustained 35-40+ degree slopes
Notoriously difficult, unmarked route-finding off-trail from Flapjack Lakes — multiple documented parties have climbed the wrong drainage/ridge
Low-5th-class/stiff-4th-class chockstone gully just below the summit, exposed and typically unprotected
Lingering snow/steep-snow in the summit gullies into early summer
Long, exposed days with few bail options — several parties describe finishing after dark

Approach trails closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire (burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall): North Fork Skokomish and Flapjack Lakes, no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026

waysIn.name: Flapjack Lakes and Sawtooth Ridge
waysIn.season: Mid-July to September
waysIn.notes: Valley trail to the lakes and usually a camp there, then off-trail into Sawtooth Ridge. Access on this side has been closed by fire damage — check the trail, not just the road. A largely abandoned line leaves the valley trail a couple of miles up and climbs the south end of the ridge; it has been in poor shape for decades. Parties pushing it car-to-car commonly report eleven to fourteen hours.
hazards: Steep loose duff and scree at 35 to 40 degrees below the ridge
A chockstone gully at low fifth class, exposed and typically unprotected
Several parallel chutes on the south face that lead into bad downclimbing
Snow in the summit gullies into early summer
Long days with few bail options and finishes after dark

name: Fremont Glacier
approach: Start at Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR 20 mile 130 (elevation 1,060 ft). Follow Thunder Creek Trail south for approximately 16-18 miles to Thunder Basin camp around 6,000 ft. From Thunder Basin, cross meadows and begin ascending. Traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, gaining approximately 2 miles to reach Fremont Glacier at 8,000 feet. Campsites exist at Thunder Basin and other designated locations along the approach.
descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, most parties can downclimb the exposed Class 3-4 summit tower and the U-notch below it with care (a belayed downclimb works for many groups), but this step is steep and exposed enough that some parties choose to rappel roughly 30-50 ft off the summit block down to the snow hogback at the glacier's upper edge rather than downclimb it with packs on. There are no fixed/bolted anchors reported on this seldom-traveled route — any rappel is built from natural gear (a rock horn or chockstone with a sling, or a picket if snow conditions allow), so carry a small rack of slings and be prepared to leave gear behind. After regaining the hogback, rope up again to reverse the Fremont Glacier crossing, drop back to high camp, then retrace the cross-country descent through Thunder Basin to rejoin the Thunder Creek Trail for the long, mostly flat hike out. The Thunder/Park Creek footlog crossings can be genuinely nerve-wracking if you're crossing them in the dark on a long summit-day exit, and the Thunder Creek ford is worth respecting if water is up.
hazards: Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier
Bergschrund forms below the summit ridge as the snow finger melts out in late season
Exposed, sometimes unroped Class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Long, unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp
Afternoon thunderstorms common in Cascades summer weather
Wildfire smoke/haze possible in August
Footlog crossings over Thunder/Park Creek are hazardous at night or high water

waysIn.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
waysIn.season: July and August
waysIn.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail south for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the Fremont Glacier saddle around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.
hazards: Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present
Bergschrund opens below the summit ridge late season as the snow finger melts, plus a moat at the crest
Exposed, often unroped Class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Steep gully through cliff bands near 7,350 ft can hold snow or ice
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp
Hazardous footlog crossings over Thunder Creek at night or high water; no fixed anchors for rappels

waysIn.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail to Park Creek Pass
waysIn.notes: From the Park Creek Trailhead on the Stehekin Valley Road, the Park Creek trail climbs to Park Creek Pass and joins the Thunder Creek line there. It needs the Lake Chelan boat and the Stehekin shuttle to reach the trailhead. The way in starts at the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, follows the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then takes the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp, with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.
hazards: Footlog crossing on Park Creek, hazardous at night or in high water
Steep gully through cliff bands near 7,350 ft above Park Creek Pass can hold snow or ice
Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present
Bergschrund opens below the summit ridge late season, plus a moat at the crest
Exposed, often unroped Class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp; no fixed anchors for rappels
waysIn.whyThisWay: To cut the Thunder Creek mileage when the boat and shuttle schedule suits you; fewer miles, but the Lake Chelan ferry, the Stehekin bus and a footlog crossing come with it.

name: Banded Glacier
approach: From the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR 20 near milepost 151, climb about 3.5 miles to the 6,500-ft pass, descend into Fisher Basin, and follow the Fisher Creek Trail down the valley to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier, about 10 miles one way. When SR 20 is closed at Easy Pass, the longer Thunder Creek way in (about 13 miles) starts at Colonial Creek Campground. In late June the Easy Pass trail can vanish under snow near the top; keep traversing west at pass level before picking up the switchbacks down to Fisher Creek.
descent: Reverse the route: descend the Banded Glacier, climb back over the col toward Fisher Creek, and hike back out over Easy Pass to the trailhead (or exit via the longer Thunder Creek Trail alternate if Easy Pass Trailhead is inaccessible).
hazards: Cliff bands above the lake camp
Crevasses on the Banded Glacier (generally avoidable on climber's left, but this can shift year to year)
Loose, chossy rock on the summit ridge
Rockfall in approach gullies
Heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin through June/July
Sustained off-trail, goat-path route-finding for the upper two-thirds of the route

waysIn.name: Easy Pass and Fisher Basin
waysIn.season: July to September; the Easy Pass trail usually holds snow until July
waysIn.notes:
The usual way in while SR 20 is open. From the Easy Pass Trailhead near milepost 151, climb about 3.5 miles to the 6,500-ft pass, drop into Fisher Basin, and follow the Fisher Creek Trail down the valley — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. About ten miles one way. The trailhead sits inside the highway's winter closure, and the pass is often snowbound until July.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge, sometimes called Christmas Tree Col, which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.
hazards: Gated trailhead tied to SR-20 seasonal closure limits when this way in is open
Crossing of a 6,500 ft pass into Fisher Basin before dropping to the lake camp
Christmas Tree Col may need a rope for steep snow; snow bridge collapse risk on the Banded Glacier
Crevasses on the Banded Glacier; talus over hard glacier ice is treacherous in a whiteout
Cliff bands above the lake camp; loose chossy summit ridge and rockfall in approach gullies
Sustained off-trail route-finding; heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin early season

waysIn.name: Thunder Creek and Fisher Creek
waysIn.season: Whenever SR 20 is closed at Easy Pass, or in the shoulder season
waysIn.notes:
The longer way in, and the one that stays open all year: the Colonial Creek trailhead is west of SR 20's winter closure gates. Take the Thunder Creek Trail from Colonial Creek Campground near 1,200 ft about nine miles to the Fisher Creek Trail junction, then the Fisher Creek Trail about three miles, past the handrailed log bridge, to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft. Roughly thirteen miles one way, with Neve Camp under two miles in for a late start.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge, sometimes called Christmas Tree Col, which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.
hazards: Major crevasse crossed on a narrow snow bridge on the Banded Glacier; snow bridge collapse near Christmas Tree Col
Christmas Tree Col may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section
Talus lying on bullet-hard glacier ice is treacherous, especially in a whiteout descent
Cliff bands above the lake camp; loose chossy rock on the summit ridge; rockfall in approach gullies
Sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding on the upper two-thirds; scree much harder to descend
Heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin through June and July
waysIn.whyThisWay: When Easy Pass is still snowbound or a party would rather not climb the steep pass; a longer all-trail walk from Colonial Creek, usually spread over several days.

name: South Route
approach: From US-2 near milepost 76 (about 11.5 miles east of Stevens Pass / 24 miles west of Leavenworth), turn onto Forest Road 657 (rough, high-clearance recommended) and drive 1.5 miles to the Merritt Lake Trailhead (3,050 ft). Hike the Merritt Lake Trail up toward the ridge, connecting with the Nason Ridge Trail; figure a long day (roughly 10 miles round trip, ~4,900 ft gain for Mastiff alone) or an overnight via Merritt or Lost Lake.
descent: Descend by the same southeast-ridge line, staying close to the ridge crest and again favoring the east side to reverse the gendarme bypass near 6,125 ft (loose rock and talus underfoot - go slow, this is the section most prone to kicking rocks onto anyone below). Where the boot path leaves the crest, follow it down through the forest to the Nason Ridge Trail, walk back about a mile to the Merritt Lake junction, and take the maintained Merritt Lake Trail down to the trailhead. This is entirely a walk-off/downclimb - no rappelling is involved anywhere on this route; the terrain throughout is Class 2-3 scrambling on talus, scree, and broken rock. The only real descent hazards are loose rock (helmet recommended, especially in groups), the boot path off the ridge fading into open heather and talus with no maintained tread - fog or flat late-day light makes it genuinely hard to relocate - and the fact that the route should not be down-climbed wet or icy since the rock gets slick.
hazards: Cornices on the south-ridge catwalk near Point 6125' — multiple failures witnessed; avoid before a solid snow-free window
Loose talus and several rock gendarmes along the summit ridge requiring careful routefinding
Cliff bands just below the ridge crest — stay close to the crest, dropping right (east) only to bypass obstacles
Bushwhacking (blueberry, alder) on off-trail sections above Merritt Lake and on any Mount Howard traverse extension
Rough, pothole/rock-strewn Forest Road 657 access — high-clearance vehicle recommended

waysIn.name: Merritt Lake Trail and Nason Ridge Trail
waysIn.season: July into October once the ridge melts out; commonly done as a long day and often paired with the neighbouring summit a mile west.
waysIn.notes: From the highway, turn north onto the signed spur for the rough forest road — high clearance is recommended — and drive to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. Self-register at the kiosk. The maintained trail switchbacks up through old-growth forest to Merritt Lake, which has established campsites and a privy and is the last dependable water before the ridge. Continue past the lake junction onto the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it north; the unsigned climbers' path toward the peak's south slopes breaks off uphill about a mile along. Above treeline the path fades into open heather and loose talus with no maintained tread and no water at all, and the ridge crest becomes the only handrail to the broad flat summit.
hazards: The route is entirely unmarked past Merritt Lake — navigation, not climbing difficulty, is the main challenge
Open heather and loose talus above treeline with no tread
Fog or whiteout makes relocating the descent path genuinely difficult
No water above Merritt Lake
One or two Class 3 moves around rock gendarmes on the crest

name: West Face
approach: Drive the paved Upper Hoh Road to its end at the Hoh Ranger Station (578 ft). Hike the Hoh River Trail 17.2 miles to Glacier Meadows (~4,200-4,300 ft), the standard base camp for this side of the range (note: a washed-out section partway up requires a fixed ladder/rope crossing). From Glacier Meadows, follow the way trail 0.8 mi to the top of the Blue Glacier lateral moraine, continue along the moraine crest ~0.2 mi, then descend onto the Blue Glacier and ascend snow slopes around rock islands to the crest of Snow Dome (6,600 ft). From Snow Dome, rope up and continue up the upper Blue Glacier to Glacier Pass (the saddle between Mathias and the East Peak of Olympus, at the head of the Hoh Glacier), then gain the base of either the Mathias snow finger or the steep gullies leading to the Mercury-Mathias col.
descent: Descend by the same line used on ascent: downclimb the Class 4 summit ridge back to the top of the snow finger, then plunge-step or downclimb the 35–40° snow finger back to Glacier Pass. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no fixed rappel stations are reported on Mathias itself, and no rappels are specifically documented for this line; treat the snow finger and the loose upper ridge as the descent crux (rockfall and a fall-arrest-consequence slope, not technical lowering). If the snow has gone to hard ice/firm neve late in the season, some parties choose to belay or downclimb facing in rather than plunge-stepping. From Glacier Pass, reverse the approach: cross back onto the Blue Glacier and descend it — passing the Snow Dome bootpack and exiting via the glacier's lateral/terminal moraine — down to Glacier Meadows Camp, and out the Hoh River Trail to the trailhead (roughly 2 days of hiking/glacier travel from Glacier Pass back to the car). Watch for rockfall on the loose upper mountain as the day warms, softening snow bridges on the Hoh/Blue Glacier crossings later in the day, and the washed-out section of the Hoh River Trail, crossed on a fixed ladder, on the way out.
hazards: remote glaciated terrain far from the road
committing multi-day access
short Class 4 exposed scrambling on the summit ridge

waysIn.name: Hoh River and the Blue Glacier to Glacier Pass
waysIn.season: Late July to mid-September
waysIn.notes: The long rainforest walk to Glacier Meadows, including a washed-out section crossed on a fixed ladder, then the way trail onto the Blue Glacier lateral moraine, across the glacier and up to Snow Dome. A multi-day Bailey Range traverse can reach Glacier Pass from the Hoh Glacier side instead. Either way this is combined with a broader trip rather than done for itself.
hazards: Hidden crevasses on the Blue and Hoh glaciers — roped travel throughout
Rockfall off the loose upper mountain as the day warms
Steep snow at 35 to 40 degrees with a fall-arrest consequence
Hard neve or ice on the finger late season, where downclimbing beats plunge-stepping
Softening snow bridges on the glacier crossings later in the day

name: North Face
approach: Long approach into the Entiat Mountains, via one of two options: from the Phelps Creek Trailhead, hike ~3.5 miles to the Leroy Creek crossing, then continue cross-country up to Leroy Basin and over the Seven Fingered Jack-Maude col; or drive Entiat River Road (becomes FR 51/5100) ~38 miles from Entiat to Cottonwood Campground, then hike the Entiat River Trail ~14.5 miles to the cirque below Maude, Seven Fingered Jack, and Fernow (this trail passes through terrain burned in the 2015 Wolverine Fire). From roughly mid-May to mid-June the Chiwawa River Road is shut at a gate for mud season, which can add many miles of road walking or biking before the Phelps Creek trailhead; in early June expect blowdowns, deep creek fords on the Phelps Creek approach and firm snow a few miles up the trail. By mid-August the glacier traverse toward the face crosses several wide-open crevasses, so rope up; a rappel station sits where the north ridge of Marmot Pyramid meets the ice, sparing a long descent onto the glacier.
descent: The North Face is not descended — after topping out on the summit ridge (9,082 ft), descend via the standard South Slopes / south ridge walk-off: down the south ridge and upper talus to about 7,700 ft, then southwest down broad open slopes to the 6,840 ft saddle. From there most parties drop back into Leroy Creek Basin to retrieve camp and reverse the Leroy Creek climber's path and Phelps Creek Trail to the trailhead; some parties instead exit via the Ice Lakes basin and the Carne Mountain High Route depending on snow conditions and where camp/vehicles are staged, which several parties describe as an efficient alternative when the Maude/Seven Fingered Jack col has gone soft and mushy in the afternoon. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required or commonly reported on the standard descent line (the single technical rappel reported is on the approach traverse under the face, not the summit descent, and is conditions-dependent rather than a fixed feature of the route). Descent-specific hazards: loose 3rd-class rock and scree on the south ridge/upper slopes, a large cornice that forms on the summit ridge above the North Face's climber's-right side (stay well back from the edge near the top), lingering steep snow and possible rockfall in the col/gully area, and — if exiting toward Ice Lakes — extra route-finding and a longer, more remote tail to the car. Parties should budget real time for this descent; one party logged roughly 13 hours car-to-car including the North Face climb and this walk-off.
hazards: frequent rockfall, especially as the face warms
bergschrund at the base
variable ice conditions
exposure

waysIn.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col
waysIn.season: Best while the face still holds continuous snow and ice, roughly Jun into mid-Jul; it used to hold year round and no longer does
waysIn.notes: Drive the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, roughly twenty-two miles and turn right onto the Phelps Creek road, FR 6211, to the trailhead at about 3,500 ft. The trail up the valley is the same tread hikers use for Spider Meadow. Walk the Phelps Creek trail, #1511, about three and a half flat miles to where it meets Leroy Creek near 4,120 to 4,140 ft. Cross on a large tree or by rock-hopping — awkward in early season with the creek up — and pick up the well-worn but unsigned climbers' trail, #1512, on the north side of the creek. It is sometimes called the Carne Mountain High Route, but the two are also treated as different paths, so do not assume the names are interchangeable. It climbs steeply, then eases into the Leroy Creek Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, roughly five miles from the car and a little over two hours for a party moving well with light packs. Good camping and water. Above the basin, one party continued on the high-route path less than a quarter mile and then went directly into the upper basin below Maude by way of a gully with a small waterfall. Keep climbing cross-country over meadow, scrub, talus and probably snow to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col at about 8,150 ft, north-west of Maude's summit.
hazards: Leroy Creek crossing on a log or by rock-hopping, awkward when running high early season
Four hundred feet of exposed descending traverse from the col on snow, ice and very loose Class 3
Sixty-degree snow for the first moves off the traverse; bergschrund at the base of the face
Cornice at the top of the face; pieces have released across parties' tracks
Frequent rockfall as the face warms; very poor rock quality across this group of peaks
Easy to descend a west-side gully by mistake instead of continuing south toward Ice Lakes

waysIn.name: Entiat River and Ice Lakes from the east — the first-ascent line
waysIn.season: Same window; this side is a much longer walk and is mostly used by parties already camped at Ice Lakes or exiting that way
waysIn.notes:
Drive the Entiat River Road and walk the Entiat River trail #1400 about eight and a quarter miles to the Ice Creek trail. The Entiat River has to be crossed on logs, and if there is no log at the trail there may be a large jam south of it.

The first-ascent party did not follow the river to the meadows at its head. They walked instead to the col between Spectacle Buttes and Maude's south-east side and dropped from Ice Lakes onto the slopes beside the face, judging it more direct and free of bushwhacking. That cost them nearly three thousand feet of climbing to reach Ice Lakes.
hazards: Unbridged crossing of the Entiat River on logs; a log jam may stand in for a missing log
Very long walk in on a trail through terrain burned by the 2015 Wolverine Fire
Bergschrund at the foot of the face on this side; crevasse crossing on the Entiat Glacier
Cornice at the top of the face; wet snow sluffing
Frequent rockfall from bordering buttresses as the face warms; variable ice conditions
Poor rock quality throughout; exposure on the face
waysIn.whyThisWay: For parties already camped at Ice Lakes or exiting that way; a far longer walk than Leroy Basin, but it reaches the face from the east without a bushwhack.

name: Nothing Couloir
approach: Same lower approach as the North Face/Entiat Icefall routes: Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft) via FR 6211, up the Phelps Creek Trail to the Leroy Creek crossing, then the climber's trail into Leroy Creek Basin (~6,100-6,200 ft, ~5 miles), continuing onto the peak's west side to reach the base of the couloir system near the standard West/South Slopes route.
descent: Descend the South Shoulder route, which pairs well with the Nothing Couloir's west-side approach to form a natural loop back down toward Leroy Creek Basin rather than reversing the climb.
hazards: Exposed class 4 moves without protection for most parties

waysIn.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the west side of the peak
waysIn.season: Aug-Sep. This is explicitly a late-season line — it wants the snow gone and the rock dry
waysIn.notes:
The lower approach is shared with the peak's north-side routes: Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft off FR-6211, Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to the Leroy Creek ford at roughly 3.5 miles, then the unmaintained Leroy Creek high route steeply up into Leroy Basin around 6,100-6,200 ft, where the established camps are. That climbers' trail gains about 1,200 ft per mile — it is short and steep and hot under an overnight pack.

Where this route parts company with its neighbours is at the basin: instead of heading for the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col or the Ice Lakes notch, it continues onto the peak's west side to reach the couloir system near the standard West / South Slopes ground.

The climb is short — roughly 450 m of mostly slabby Class 3 with two brief Class 4 steps — and it pairs naturally with a descent of the South Shoulder to make a loop back into Leroy Basin rather than a there-and-back.
hazards: Loose rock among the summit-ridge towers on the traverse south
Brief exposed Class 4 moves that most parties climb without protection
Miscounting the gullies from the North Tower, which puts you on unrecorded ground on the same face
A steep unmaintained climbers' trail into Leroy Basin gaining roughly 1,200 ft per mile
A late-season route on an east-side peak, so afternoon thunderstorms and smoke are the normal conditions

name: North Slopes from Lake Valhalla
approach: From US Highway 2 about 4 miles east of Stevens Pass, turn onto Smith Brook Road (Forest Road 6700) and follow the gravel road roughly 2.6-2.8 miles to the Smithbrook Trailhead (el. ~4,000 ft; no fee, no Northwest Forest Pass required); the road is closed to vehicles under a storm-damage order effective May 20, 2026 through December 31, 2027 unless lifted sooner, so confirm it has reopened before driving. Hike Smithbrook Trail #1590 through old-growth forest, entering the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness at about 0.5 mile, and continue to Union Gap (el. ~4,600-4,688 ft) at roughly 1.0-1.3 miles, where the trail meets the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn south (left) on the PCT for about 1.4 miles through forest with views toward Lichtenberg Mountain and Nason Ridge, to an unnamed gap at about 5,100 ft. Just before/at this gap, an unmarked but obvious boot path breaks off to the north through heather meadows, climbing a steep, sometimes brushy and eroded 0.5 mile (about 650 ft of additional gain) to the true summit.
descent: Retrace the steep climber's path back to the PCT/Smithbrook junction, then follow the PCT and Smithbrook Trail out to the trailhead.
hazards: loose talus and dirt
early-season snow
unmarked, braided boot path (route-finding)

waysIn.name: Smithbrook Trail to Union Gap and the Lake Valhalla crest trail
waysIn.season: July through October is the dependable window; the access road holds snow into early summer.
waysIn.notes: From the highway east of the pass, take the gravel forest road (closed to vehicles under a storm-damage order through December 31, 2027 unless lifted sooner) to the Smithbrook Trailhead and self-register for wilderness travel. Smithbrook Trail #1590 climbs through brush and an old boulder field and then old-growth forest, entering the wilderness within the first half mile, and tops out at Union Gap on the crest trail. Turn south onto a relatively flat, blueberry- and huckleberry-lined stretch with views toward the neighbouring peak and the ridge beyond. The trail runs through forest to an unnamed gap before it begins its drop toward Lake Valhalla, and it is at that gap that the climbers' path leaves it and turns north up the open slope.
hazards: The turnoff carries no sign of any kind and the tread reads as a gully rather than a trail
The climbers' path braids into several social paths with no signage — pick the one that visibly heads for the summit
Lingering snow patches cross the path into early summer and can bury the tread
Steep and eroded going, with sections where you shimmy through foliage
The summit ridge carries a brief drop and reclimb before the true top, so the first crest is not it

name: Standard Scramble (Deception Creek / Royal Basin)
approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (Forest Road 2870, Olympic National Forest), follow the Upper Dungeness Trail (#833.2) about 1 mile, then Royal Creek Trail (#832) into Buckhorn Wilderness and across the park boundary to Royal Lake / Royal Basin (roughly 6-7 miles and ~2,500 ft of gain from the trailhead). From upper Royal Basin, continue off-trail cross-country over Royal Pass (~6,500 ft) into Deception Basin, then up basins/gullies (via the Mystery Glacier or the south ridge) to the base of the summit block. Expect a multi-day backcountry trip for most parties.
descent: Reverse the ascent line. The technical crux is downclimbing back from the summit block to the south ridge notch through the same loose, exposed class 3–4 gully; some parties make two single-rope rappels from near the summit down to the saddle/notch rather than downclimbing the whole thing, then downclimbing the remaining class 2–3 terrain. A single 60m rope is sufficient for each of the two rappels; no bolted or fixed hardware is reported anywhere on this remote, seldom-traveled Olympic National Park peak, so anchors should be assumed natural (slung horns, chockstones, or gear placements) — build and back these up carefully given the rotten rock. Below the notch, downclimb/scramble the mixed rock-and-snow traverse back to the top of Mystery Glacier, then descend the low-angle glacier (parties commonly glissade or down-scramble it quickly in good conditions) back to the Deception Basin camp/gravel bars. From Deception Basin, re-climb the loose scree traverse to the Royal/Deception divide and descend the 35–40° snow slope back into Upper Royal Basin — many glissade this if runout is clean, but check for exposed rock in late season since a fall here would run a long way. From Upper Royal Basin, follow the maintained Royal Basin/Upper Dungeness Trail back down past Royal Lake to the trailhead. Note: a different, longer traverse exit continues past the south ridge notch over Gunsight Pass toward Constance Pass and out the Dosewallips/Del Monte Ridge trail system with no rappels required — that is a valid but distinct high-route variant, not the standard reverse-the-ascent descent described above.
hazards: Rotten, tilted pillow-basalt rock that breaks away readily
Steep, exposed scrambling on the summit block, with brief Class 4 moves possible depending on line, and serious fall consequences
Lingering steep snow on the approach gullies and Mystery Glacier into summer

A solo backcountry traveler (Sean Allen, 38) died in a fall near the peak's south end / Del Monte ridgeline in July 2022, a reminder of the terrain and weather risk here — the death was ruled an accidental fall

waysIn.name: Upper Dungeness and Royal Basin, over the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The notch below the divide holds 35-40 degree snow and an axe is worth carrying outside late season
waysIn.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead on FR-2870 — large parking area, vault toilet; an overnight stay needs an Olympic National Park wilderness permit booked in advance — take Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 about a mile. The trail forks just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge; bear right onto the Royal Basin Trail #832. A short way up, stay left where the Maynard Burn Way branches off; it is easy to mistake in early light.

Royal Creek Camp, about 4 miles in, is a common first night. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the main basecamp, with designated sites and a seasonal ranger post — the last dependable water before the dry climb. Many parties push on to camps around 5,800-6,200 ft in upper Royal Basin.

From upper Royal Basin, climb a moraine and a snowfield of roughly 35-40 degrees to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend shower-tile scree to grass and heather benches above Deception Basin.
hazards: Rotten, tilted pillow basalt that breaks away readily, with rockfall funnelled by the gullies above the col
A Class 4 step on poor rock over steep runout dirt that must be reversed on descent — one party graded a move on the downclimb at 5.8
A reported moat over 30 ft deep below the gully late in the season
Lingering steep snow on the approach gullies and Mystery Glacier into summer, and a 35-40 degree snow slope below the Royal-Deception notch
Remote terrain — a solo traveller died in a fall near the peak's south end in July 2022

waysIn.name: Home Lake and Constance Pass, reaching Deception Basin from the south
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
waysIn.notes:
The other side, and the one that suits a party already camped at Home Lake for Fricaba or Warrior. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, Trail #833.2 to Camp Handy at about 3.4 miles and Boulder Shelter at about 6.4 miles and 4,890 ft, then the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail to Home Lake at roughly 9.3 miles and 5,308-5,330 ft. From camp, climbers' paths lead up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, and from there the route traverses and descends west into upper Deception Basin.

This is the same basin the Royal Basin parties drop into, reached from the opposite end. It is the approach a high-route party is already on, and one detailed account describes exiting this way over Gunsight Pass toward Constance Pass and out the Dosewallips and Del Monte Ridge trail system with no rappels — a valid variant exit, distinct from reversing the ascent.
hazards: Loose scree traverses between Constance Pass and Deception Basin
All the summit-block hazards of the standard variant, including the reversible Class 4 step
Steep snow lingering on the Constance Pass and Deception Basin traverse into July
Long committing backcountry travel far from help
waysIn.whyThisWay: When already camped at Home Lake for a neighbouring peak, or when linking into a longer high route or loop, this reaches the same basin from the south instead of via Royal Basin.

name: Standard Scramble
approach: Multi-day approach: hike the Skokomish Lower/Upper South Fork Trail (Olympic National Forest Trail #873) to the Six Ridge Trail and Sundown Pass/Lake, then follow the primitive "Mount Olson Way" boot path along Six Ridge off-trail to Olson's upper slopes. Expect significant brush and blowdowns low, easier scrambling higher up.
descent: From the pass immediately east of the summit, the final climb to Mount Olson's 5,289 ft high point is a steep, unmarked scramble up a grassy/heather slope pitched around 55-60 degrees in places — hands-on, solid Class 3 — that eases and curves around the north side of the peak on a heather bench before an easy stroll to the true summit. There is no fixed hardware, cairned rappel station, or reported roped descent anywhere on this peak: parties down-climb the exact line they climbed. Descend the steep meadow/heather pitch back to the east pass, drop back into Success Basin, pass the tarn again, and reverse the loose notch/talus crossing back up and over to Camp Belview — treat the notch and the upper summit meadow as the descent crux, since both are loose, exposed, and best handled with an ice axe or trekking pole for self-arrest, especially if wet or carrying late-season snow. From Camp Belview, retrace the Six Ridge Trail through its repeated ridge crossings to Six Ridge Pass, down to Sundown Lake, back over Sundown Pass, and down the South Fork Skokomish River Trail to the trailhead — essentially the same multi-day return as the approach, in reverse. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappelling: rappels = 0.
hazards: routefinding on trail-less/boot-path terrain
dense brush and blowdowns along the Six Ridge approach
afternoon weather

waysIn.name: South Fork Skokomish Trail #873 to Sundown Pass, then the Six Ridge crest and the Mount Olson Way
waysIn.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and gated by river fords that are only reliably safe in late summer and early autumn low water
waysIn.notes:
Mount Olson sees very few ascents and is normally reached as a side trip off the long Six Ridge traverse. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish Trailhead (Trail #873), reached via Skokomish Valley Road, FS-23 and FS-2361 from Shelton — FS-2361 is gated 1 October to 30 April — the trail runs up the valley. There is an unbridged ford of the South Fork at about 2.4 miles and 1,450 ft that is only ankle-deep and safely crossable in late summer or early autumn low water; at other times it is a serious hazard. The Olympic National Park boundary comes near 5.1 miles, after which tread grows fainter and an advance-reserved wilderness permit is required for overnight stays.

Sundown Pass, a forested saddle marked by a broken signpost, comes at about 7.2 miles and 4,125 ft. The trail drops on to Lake Sundown at about 7.6 miles and 3,810 ft, a designated camp where the Six Ridge Trail begins, climbing about 800 ft to Six Ridge Pass; small streams toward McGravey Lakes and a spring at Belview Camp further along the ridge also supply water.

Follow the Six Ridge Trail east along its sawtooth crest — a ridge either side with a gully in the middle, and brutal uphill for every downhill — past McGravey Lakes to Belview Camp at about 4,400 ft, where an unsigned, unofficial boot path known as the Mount Olson way leaves the trail for the peak. It is faint and overgrown with blowdown and lingering snowfields into midsummer. A boulder-field tarn at about 5,100 ft below the summit block is the last water and a common bivy.
hazards: Unbridged fords of the South Fork, only safely crossable in late summer and early autumn low water
Route-finding on trail-less and boot-path terrain with an unsigned departure from Six Ridge
Dense brush and blowdown along the Six Ridge approach
A 55-60 degree grass and heather summit pitch that is loose and exposed, and worse descending
FS-2361 is gated 1 October to 30 April
Afternoon weather on an exposed crest, and a multi-day return from a very lightly visited peak
